course.title: Creative and Game Writing
course.description: Learn how stories work and how to write them, from character and scene to dialogue and point of view, then apply the same craft to games with branching and reactive narrative.
course.audience: A capable adult who reads fiction or plays story-driven games and wants to write their own. Comfortable writing sentences; no creative-writing training assumed. Some basic comfort with if-then logic helps in the last third, but programming is not required.

paragraphs: A reader seldom keeps turning the pages because of the events alone, since a list of things that happen, however dramatic, gives us no reason to want the next one. We read on because someone in the story wants something and can't easily have it, and because each event happens as a result of the one before, so that we want to know where the chain will lead. Creative writing is the craft of building that chain on purpose, and once you can see it you can say why a draft drags, or why a scene that looked fine on the page falls flat when it is read.

Games add a problem the page never has, because the player acts. The writer can't know in advance which door will be opened, which character will be trusted or whether a cutscene will be watched at all, so writing for a game means planning for every path a player might take and for every line they might hear more than once. That turns some questions of craft into questions you can settle by counting, such as how many passages a branching story needs or how many lines a fight needs before a player hears one again, and it lets you decide what a story should remember about the player before you write a word of it.
outcomes: You'll be able to explain why a sequence of events becomes a story, and state a protagonist's want, obstacle and change.
You'll be able to compare three-act, five-part and four-part story structures and place events in them.
You'll be able to build a character from want, need, flaw and choices under pressure.
You'll be able to shape a scene around a goal, a conflict and a turning point.
You'll be able to write dialogue with subtext and distinct voices, and choose a point of view on purpose.
You'll be able to sketch a branching structure, count its writing cost, and track state with variables.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on English: Reading, Writing and Rhetoric.
introduction.length: 12 lessons, about 12 to 15 minutes each. Each ends with an optional writing task of 5 to 15 minutes.

modules.title: The shape of a story
modules.description: What turns events into a story, how stories are structured, and who is in them.

modules.title: Scene and sentence
modules.description: Writing the scene as a unit, then dialogue, point of view and revision.

modules.title: Writing for games
modules.description: What changes when the reader acts: agency, branching structure, state, game text and consequence.

concepts.title: Story and plot
concepts.summary: A story is events in time order; a plot links them by cause, so the second event happens because of the first.

concepts.title: Want
concepts.summary: A want is what a character is trying to get in the story, and it gives events a direction.

concepts.title: Obstacle
concepts.summary: An obstacle is whatever stands between the character and the want, and it makes the effort cost something.

concepts.title: Change
concepts.summary: A change is a difference between the character's situation or belief at the start and at the end.

concepts.title: Stakes
concepts.summary: Stakes are what the character stands to lose if the want fails.

concepts.title: Beginning, middle and end
concepts.summary: Aristotle's Poetics defines a whole as having a beginning, a middle and an end, each following necessarily from what came before.

concepts.title: Three-act structure
concepts.summary: Three-act structure divides a story into setup, confrontation and resolution; in a screenplay the acts are conventionally about 25, 50 and 25 percent.

concepts.title: Freytag's pyramid
concepts.summary: Freytag's five parts are exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and catastrophe (denouement).

concepts.title: Kishotenketsu
concepts.summary: Kishotenketsu has four parts: ki (introduction), sho (development), ten (twist) and ketsu (conclusion), and does not depend on conflict.

concepts.title: The hero's journey
concepts.summary: Joseph Campbell described a recurring departure, initiation and return pattern in myth, which Christopher Vogler later reduced to twelve stages for film.

concepts.title: Want and need
concepts.summary: A want is what the character pursues; a need is what the character must come to see or do to change, and the two often conflict.

concepts.title: Flaw
concepts.summary: A flaw is a habit or belief that works against the want, and it explains why the obstacle is hard for this character.

concepts.title: Choice under pressure
concepts.summary: A character is revealed by what they choose when the choice costs them.

concepts.title: Agency
concepts.summary: A character has agency when the events of the plot follow from their decisions.

concepts.title: Contradiction
concepts.summary: Specific contradictions, such as a generous miser, make characters feel like people.

concepts.title: Scene goal
concepts.summary: A scene goal is what the point-of-view character wants right now, small enough to be won or lost in the scene.

concepts.title: Scene conflict
concepts.summary: Conflict is the resistance to that goal, from another character, the situation or the character's own hesitation.

concepts.title: Turning point
concepts.summary: A turning point is the moment the situation changes direction, so the scene ends differently from how it began.

concepts.title: Outcome
concepts.summary: A scene outcome is usually a failure or a success with a cost, which pushes the next scene.

concepts.title: Enter late, leave early
concepts.summary: Start the scene as close to the conflict as possible and end it as soon as the turn has landed.

concepts.title: Subtext
concepts.summary: Subtext is meaning beneath what is said, so a line can mean more than its words.

concepts.title: Voice
concepts.summary: Characters differ in vocabulary, rhythm, sentence length and what they avoid saying.

concepts.title: Tags and beats
concepts.summary: A tag attributes a line ('she said'); a beat is an action between lines that shows what the speaker is doing or feeling.

concepts.title: Expository dialogue
concepts.summary: Dialogue where characters tell each other what both already know, only to inform the reader, reads as false.

concepts.title: Compression
concepts.summary: Real speech is full of filler; dialogue on the page keeps what the scene needs.

concepts.title: First person
concepts.summary: First person tells the story as 'I', limited to what the narrator knows, perceives and chooses to say.

concepts.title: Second person
concepts.summary: Second person addresses 'you', common in interactive fiction because the reader acts.

concepts.title: Close third
concepts.summary: Close third uses 'he' or 'she' but stays inside one character's perceptions at a time.

concepts.title: Omniscient
concepts.summary: An omniscient narrator can enter any character's mind and describe events the characters cannot see.

concepts.title: Unreliable narrator
concepts.summary: An unreliable narrator tells the story in a way the reader learns not to trust.

concepts.title: Specific detail
concepts.summary: A specific detail is a concrete, sensory and chosen thing that implies a general truth without stating it.

concepts.title: Showing and telling
concepts.summary: Telling states a conclusion; showing gives evidence from which the reader draws it, and a good story uses both.

concepts.title: Revision passes
concepts.summary: Revise in order from largest to smallest: structure, scene, then line, because fixing sentences in a scene that will be cut wastes effort.

concepts.title: Cutting
concepts.summary: Most drafts improve when cut by a fifth to a quarter, removing repeats and restated points.

concepts.title: Reading aloud
concepts.summary: Reading aloud exposes rhythm problems that silent reading skips.

concepts.title: Player agency
concepts.summary: Player agency is the ability to make choices that matter to the game's events.

concepts.title: Four narrative types
concepts.summary: Henry Jenkins (2004) described evoked, enacted, embedded and emergent narrative: stories that rely on prior knowledge, stories the player performs, stories placed in the world, and stories that arise from play.

concepts.title: Ludonarrative dissonance
concepts.summary: Ludonarrative dissonance, a term from Clint Hocking (2007), is a conflict between what the story says and what the mechanics reward.

concepts.title: Environmental storytelling
concepts.summary: Environmental storytelling puts story in the arrangement of the world, such as a room that shows what happened there.

concepts.title: Cutscene and gameplay
concepts.summary: Cutscenes give the writer control, and gameplay gives the player control; good game writing moves between the two.

concepts.title: Branching
concepts.summary: Branching gives the player choices that lead to different passages.

concepts.title: Branching tree
concepts.summary: A branching tree never rejoins, so n binary choices give 2^n endings.

concepts.title: Branch and bottleneck
concepts.summary: In branch and bottleneck, branches rejoin at shared passages, which limits the amount of text.

concepts.title: Hub
concepts.summary: A hub structure returns the player to a central passage from several optional strands.

concepts.title: Writing cost
concepts.summary: The number of passages a structure needs, not its number of endings, is its writing cost.

concepts.title: Variable
concepts.summary: A variable stores a value, such as a number, a true or false flag or a name, and can change as the story proceeds.

concepts.title: Flag
concepts.summary: A flag is a true-or-false variable recording that something happened.

concepts.title: Condition
concepts.summary: A condition tests a variable and decides which text appears or which choices are offered.

concepts.title: State space
concepts.summary: With n independent flags there are 2^n possible combinations, so tracked state grows quickly.

concepts.title: ink script
concepts.summary: In ink, VAR declares a variable, a line starting with ~ changes it, a line starting with * offers a choice, and { condition: A | B } shows A if the condition is true and B otherwise.

concepts.title: Bark
concepts.summary: A bark is a short line triggered by an event, such as a guard's 'Over here!'.

concepts.title: Repetition budget
concepts.summary: The number of distinct lines needed is the rate of play divided into the time, so that the player does not hear the same line twice in a window.

concepts.title: Quest text
concepts.summary: Quest text tells the player what to do and where, in as few words as possible, with story kept in the quest's reasons.

concepts.title: String limits and expansion
concepts.summary: Interface strings have length limits, and translation may lengthen them; a common allowance is about 30 percent for languages longer than English.

concepts.title: Interruptibility
concepts.summary: Lines must make sense when cut off, skipped, or heard out of order.

concepts.title: Meaningful choice
concepts.summary: A choice is meaningful when the options are clearly different, the player can predict something about their effects, and the game later responds.

concepts.title: Delayed consequence
concepts.summary: A delayed consequence shows the effect of an earlier choice in a later scene.

concepts.title: Reactive text
concepts.summary: Reactive text changes a few lines to acknowledge a choice, without a new branch.

concepts.title: Pacing
concepts.summary: Pacing in a branching story balances choice frequency with passage length, so the player is neither idle nor overloaded.

concepts.title: Word budget
concepts.summary: A word budget fixes how many words each shared and branching passage may use.

lead.text: Look at the first view of the figure. Ana's bridge fails its inspection, the town closes it, her bakery loses customers, and so on to a queue at the market. Every event is there, and they come in order, but the only thing an arrow between neighbours can say is *then*. Forster called events arranged in time order a **story**.

Now switch to the second view, where the same arrows say *so*. The town closed the bridge because it failed, the bakery lost customers because the bridge was closed, and Ana bought a cart oven because she needed some way to reach them. When events are joined by cause we call the result a **plot**, and that is exactly the difference 'of grief' makes in Forster's sentences.

afterFigure.text: The cause matters to a reader because of what it makes us do. After a list we have no particular reason to want the next item, but after a chain of causes we want to know what the last event will lead to. Forster put it as two questions, since a story makes us ask “and then?” while a plot makes us ask “why?”.

lead.text: Ana wants to keep her bakery open, and that one sentence turns a closed bridge from an inconvenience into a threat. We call what a character is trying to get in the story a **want**, and it is the most dependable source of cause there is: the character acts, the world answers, and the character has to act again.

afterFigure.text: The second view shows the **obstacle**, whatever stands between the character and the want. The third view adds the **stakes**, what the character stands to lose if the want fails. Ana lives above the shop, so losing the bakery means losing her home too, and that is why we care whether she gets across.

reveal.text: The storm blocks her, and nobody is behind it. An obstacle can be weather, a place, the clock, a fear, or a belief the character holds, and the next screen takes those in turn.

lead.text: It is easy to think that every story needs a villain, because the stories we meet first have one. Look at what an obstacle has to do, though: it has to stand between the character and the want, so that getting the want costs effort. A villain does that, and so does a storm. A fear does it too, as when a diver wants the prize and is afraid of deep water. So does the clock, when a surgeon has one hour. So does a belief, when a woman wants to apologise and has decided that she never will.

The last kind is often the most interesting, because the character is then the one blocking the want. Whenever you find a want with no obstacle, you have found a place where the character could simply have what they asked for and the story stops.

How do we know a story has finished? One answer is that it has delivered a **change**, a difference between the character's situation or belief at the start and at the end. The change can be outward, as when Ana ends up with a market stall instead of a shop, or inward, as when a character stops believing something they believed at the start.
The table shows three short summaries, each reduced to a want, an obstacle and a change.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the change in each row answers the want and the obstacle together. A change that ignores both of them would feel as if it belonged to another story.

steps.headline: Reduce Ana's story to three sentences, one for the want, one for the obstacle and one for the change.

workedSteps.text: Start with the want. It is what the character is trying to get, so write it as an action Ana could be seen taking.
workedSteps.math: Want: Ana wants to keep her bakery open.

workedSteps.text: Next find whatever stands between her and that, which in this story is not a person.
workedSteps.math: Obstacle: the town closes the only bridge to her customers.

workedSteps.text: Then look at the end of the story and compare it with the start, asking what is different about Ana.
workedSteps.math: Change: she ends as a baker with a queue at a market stall instead of a shop.

workedSteps.text: Last, check that the change answers the want and the obstacle, since the cart oven is what lets her reach customers across the closed bridge.

steps.headline: Finish the three sentences for Tomas, a night cleaner who wants a clerk's job at the bank.

workedSteps.text: Tomas wants to be hired as a clerk, but the bank hires only people with a diploma. At forty he sits the exam and passes, and by the end he no longer thinks of himself as someone who cleans up after others. The want is the job he is trying to get.
workedSteps.math: Want: a clerk's job at the bank.

workedSteps.text: The obstacle is what blocks him, and here it is a missing piece of paper, not a person.
Now compare the end of the story with its start.

reveal.text: The sentence says nothing about happiness, and a change was never a promise of it. She started with a friend and ends without one, and that difference is the change.

Each event in a plot leans on the one before it, so taking out a cause leaves the next event unexplained, and the reader feels the gap as a jump. To cut an event, you either keep what it caused out of the story too or give that next event a new cause.

lessons.orientation: Say what separates a story from a list of events, and state a protagonist's want, obstacle and change in three sentences.
lessons.nextAction: Compare three-act, five-part and four-part structures and place events within them.

blocks.text: Here are two sentences about a king and a queen. The first is “The king died and then the queen died.” The second is “The king died, and then the queen died of grief.” Both report the same two deaths in the same order, and yet E. M. Forster, lecturing on the novel in 1927, called the first a story and the second a plot. The only difference between them is two words, *of grief*.

Why should two words matter so much? They add no event, since the queen dies in both sentences. What they change is the way we read her death, and once you can say what that change is, you can say what any story needs before a reader will follow it, whether it is printed on a page or played in a game.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what turns a list of events into a story, and to state a character's want, obstacle and change in three sentences.
intro.whyItMatters: A draft that has a want, an obstacle and a change can be fixed. A draft that lacks one has no shape to fix.

recap.keyIdea: A plot is made of events joined by cause, and a story that works gives its character a want, an obstacle in the way and a change by the end.

blocks.text: Forster's king and queen showed us that two events in order make a story, and that a cause between them makes a plot. The cause comes from a character's want, from the obstacle that makes getting it cost something, and from the stakes that say what failure would take. When the ending differs from the start, whether for better or worse, the character has changed, and you can test any draft by writing those three parts in three sentences.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the shapes that events can be arranged in, from three acts to five parts to a four-part form that needs no conflict.

lessons.title: Story structure

lead.text: Start with Aristotle, who wrote in the *Poetics* that a whole thing has a “beginning, middle, and end”. That sounds too obvious to need saying, but he meant that the parts depend on each other: the beginning needs nothing before it, the end needs nothing after it, and the middle needs both. Modern screenwriting guides keep the three-part shape, call the parts **acts**, and give them rough proportions, which the figure lays out on a 120-page script.

afterFigure.text: Treat these figures as a **convention**, a habit that teachers pass on, and not as a law, since the percentages only tell you where an audience used to the form expects the story to turn.

reveal.text: On the convention, act two would begin a quarter of the way through 120 pages, on page 30, and end three quarters of the way through, on page 90. A late turn is a choice to make knowingly, since an audience used to the form will feel the setup running long whether or not the writer meant it to.

lead.text: Three parts say little about what happens inside the middle, and in 1863 Gustav Freytag offered a finer description of drama in *Die Technik des Dramas*. He saw five parts arranged like a pyramid, which the figure draws. The **exposition** sets out the situation, the **rising action** piles up complications, the **climax** is the turning point at the top, the **falling action** carries the consequences of that turn, and the **catastrophe** is the outcome that ends the drama. Freytag was describing tragedy, which is why his last part has that name, and for a story with a happy ending it is often simply called the resolution.

afterFigure.text: Look at where the top of the pyramid sits. People often use “climax” to mean the last big scene, but in Freytag's model it is the turning point in the middle, and two parts still follow it. A story can keep us gripped after its climax in this sense, because the climax is where the situation turns and the falling action is where we find out what the turn costs.

lead.text: Not every tradition builds a story around opposed forces. A four-part pattern usually traced to classical Chinese poetry, and taught in Japanese writing classes as **kishotenketsu**, works differently. *Ki* introduces the people and the place, *sho* develops what was introduced, *ten* brings in a twist, and *ketsu* draws the pieces together. The figure gives a four-panel example, written for this lesson, about a man who feeds a stray cat.

afterFigure.text: Nothing in the first two panels is in conflict, and yet the story holds our attention, because the third panel tells us that six households feed the same cat. That twist works by making us read ki and sho again with a different meaning, as the second view shows. Freytag builds interest from forces that oppose each other until the climax, and kishotenketsu builds it from a change in how we see what we've already been shown.

steps.headline: Place the events of the fable of the hare and the tortoise into Freytag's five parts.

workedSteps.text: The hare mocks the tortoise for being slow, and the tortoise answers by challenging him to a race. This sets out the people and the situation.
The race begins, the hare sprints ahead, and sure of winning he lies down for a nap. Complications and the hare's confidence both keep growing.
The tortoise plods past the sleeping hare, and the favourite is suddenly behind.
The hare wakes and runs, but he is too far back, and we see what his nap has cost him.
The tortoise crosses the line first. This is the outcome that ends the fable.

steps.headline: Place the end of act two in a 96-page script, using the 25, 50 and 25 percent convention.

workedSteps.text: Act one ends at 25 percent of the script, which is a quarter of 96 pages.
Act two takes the next 50 percent, so it ends where 75 percent of the script has gone by.
Act two therefore ends once 75 percent of the 96 pages have gone by.

lead.text: A fourth shape comes from comparative myth. Joseph Campbell described a pattern in *The Hero with a Thousand Faces* (1949) in which a hero leaves home, is tested far away and comes back changed.

The pattern fits many stories and fits quite a few badly. So treat the three acts, the pyramid, kishotenketsu and the hero's journey as lenses. Each one shows you something a draft is doing, and a draft that fits none of them is not wrong for that reason.

reveal.text: The pyramid has the climax in the middle, with two parts before it and two after, so a list that starts or ends with the climax cannot be right.

lessons.orientation: Compare three-act, five-part and four-part story structures and place events within them.
lessons.nextAction: Build a character from want, need, flaw and a costly choice.

blocks.text: Open almost any guide to screenwriting and you'll find a number: the first act of a feature film ends about a quarter of the way through, and the second act ends about three quarters of the way through. Writers plan whole scripts around those two points, and script readers check where a story turns before they read much else. Is that how stories have to be built?

It isn't, and seeing why is useful, because the quarter-way rule is a habit of one industry, describing where film audiences have learned to expect a story to change direction. Other traditions cut a story into different parts, and one of them builds a satisfying story without any conflict at all.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place the events of a story in three acts, in Freytag's five parts and in the four parts of kishotenketsu.
intro.whyItMatters: Each structure shows a draft from a different angle, so you can see where a story sags before readers do.

recap.keyIdea: Three-act, five-part and four-part structures are different descriptions of how stories are shaped, and none of them is a recipe.

blocks.text: Aristotle's beginning, middle and end became three acts, which screenwriting guides give the proportions 25, 50 and 25 percent as a convention. Freytag's pyramid has five parts and puts its climax in the middle, with the falling action and catastrophe still to come, while kishotenketsu has four parts and builds on a twist in the third. The hero's journey adds a pattern drawn from myth, and each one describes what stories often do without deciding what yours has to.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from the shape of a whole story to the person it happens to, and asks how a character is built from want, need, flaw and choices.

lessons.title: Character

lead.text: Aristotle made the point in the *Poetics*: character, he said, “reveals moral purpose, showing what kind of things a man chooses or avoids”. In other words, we find out who someone is from what they choose.

afterFigure.text: Choice reveals character only when it costs something. In the figure, going back for the dog costs Mara her hands and her tools, and staying out costs her the dog and her good opinion of herself. If one of the two branches were free, there would be no decision to watch, and so a **choice under pressure** is one in which every option costs the character something they care about.

diagram.alt: A decision diagram: Mara hears a dog inside a burning shed and either goes back in for it or stays out. The second view adds a cost to each branch.

lead.text: Start with Nell, a thief. Her **want** is money enough to leave the city, and it is what she is chasing. But she cannot get out alone, because the job needs a partner, and what she lacks is trust in one other person. We call what a character lacks to be whole a **need**, and a good story often makes the need different from the want, with the character unaware of it for a long time.

Between the two stands a **flaw**, a belief or habit that keeps the need out of reach. Nell tells no one her plans, and that habit has served her well, and it is also exactly what stops her trusting a partner.

lead.text: A mercenary who works for pay is a type, and we have met a hundred of them. A mercenary who keeps stopping to help strangers is someone in particular, because her traits pull against each other and we want to know which will win. We call a trait that pulls against a character's others a **contradiction**.

In *Aspects of the Novel* E. M. Forster described a round character as one that is “capable of surprising in a convincing way”. The surprise has to be convincing, so the contradiction cannot be arbitrary: Tessa's kindness has to cost her something and sit oddly with her trade, and in time we should see why she cannot help it.

If events happen *to* a character, the character has no say in them, and the story starts to feel like a ride. We say a character has **agency** when the plot turns on what they decide. A simple test is to list the major events and ask of each whether the character could have prevented it, caused it or chosen it.

Two other mistakes are worth naming, because they feel like depth and are not. One is a tragic backstory, which explains a character but gives them no decision to make now. The other is a list of traits, which describes without showing.

reveal.text: Two of eight is a quarter of the major events, which leaves her a passenger for most of the story. Raising it usually means moving a decision, and not an event, into the middle of the scene.

steps.headline: Build a short character sheet for Joss, a ferry mechanic, one row at a time.

workedSteps.text: Begin with what she is chasing. Joss wants to buy back her father's workshop.
Then find what she lacks. She has done every repair alone for years, and what she lacks is someone she can rely on.
workedSteps.math: Need: to let someone help her

workedSteps.text: Next comes what Joss believes about asking for help: that asking means owing a debt.
Add a trait that pulls against the rest, so that she is not simply one thing.
workedSteps.math: Contradiction: lends her tools to anyone, and accepts a lift from no one

workedSteps.text: Last, write a situation that forces a choice between the want and the need, with a cost on each side.
workedSteps.math: Defining choice: take the workshop money from a rival, or let her apprentice repair the engine and take the credit

steps.headline: Write the defining choice for Tessa, the mercenary who wants pay but keeps helping strangers.

workedSteps.text: Tessa's want is pay, and her contradiction is that she stops to help strangers.
The last row of the sheet is the defining choice.

reveal.text: Backstory is a reason, and a choice is evidence. Making her do something that costs her now will say more than another paragraph about her past.

lessons.orientation: Build a character from want, need, flaw and a defining choice, and say what a choice under pressure shows.
lessons.nextAction: Shape a scene around a goal, a conflict and a turning point.

blocks.text: Here are two sentences about the same woman. One says “Mara is brave.” The other says “Mara went back for the dog while the roof was coming down.” Both tell us she has courage, but only the second lets us watch her pay for it, and a reader who meets both will believe the second and forget the first.

Aristotle argued in the *Poetics* that we learn what a person is like from what they choose, and that claim is still the most practical thing a writer can know about **character**. If a choice reveals more than any description can, then building a character is mostly a matter of deciding what they want, what they lack and which choice will force them to pick between the two, and of making sure the plot turns on that choice.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to build a character from a want, a need, a flaw and a costly choice, and say what a choice under pressure shows that a description cannot.
intro.whyItMatters: Readers believe a character from what they do under pressure, so the choices you plan matter more than the adjectives.

recap.keyIdea: A character is shown by what they choose when every option costs them something, and not by the traits we are told they have.

blocks.text: A want says what the character is chasing, a need says what they lack, and a flaw is the habit that keeps the need out of reach, so the sheet already holds the shape of a story. A contradiction makes the character specific, and agency makes sure the plot turns on their decisions. When you want to show who someone is, write the choice at which the want and the need pull apart, and make both sides cost.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes those choices into scenes, where a goal, a conflict and a turning point shape each unit of the story.

lessons.title: The scene

lead.text: Take the cook who asks the owner of a restaurant for a raise. A place does not make this a scene, since the same kitchen could hold ten scenes and none. What makes it one is that the cook is after something and someone stands in the way. The cook's **scene goal** is the raise, which is smaller than the story's want and serves it. The **conflict** is the opposition, and here it is the owner, who has just lost money and says so.

afterFigure.text: The line in the figure follows the cook's hope. Then the owner proposes a share in the restaurant in place of a raise, and hope leaps up. That moment, where the value the scene is about changes direction, is the **turning point**. The scene ends with an **outcome**, and here it is success with a cost, since a share also means a share of the debts.

reveal.text: A turning point is the line where the value flips, and it can arrive in the middle of what seems like good news.

lead.text: How do you recognise a turning point in your own draft? Name the value the scene is about, such as hope, safety or trust, and ask where it changes sign. In the cook's scene the value is hope for the raise, and it flips twice. Putting numbers on the value can help when you plan: if we say hope runs from −3 to +3, a scene that begins at +1 and ends at −2 has moved three points, and a scene that begins and ends at +1 has not moved at all.

The outcome does not have to settle anything. We might expect a scene to resolve what it raises, and many do, but the cook's does not: she gets a share, and the share brings her into the owner's debts. Good outcomes often take the form *yes, but* or *no, and what is more*, because an outcome that raises a larger problem is what makes the reader want the next scene.

reveal.text: A value can move a long way without turning, as when despair deepens from −1 to −3, so the test for a turning point is whether the value changes sign, not how far it travels.

lead.text: Dwight Swain, in *Techniques of the Selling Writer*, gave this account a second half. His scene runs goal, conflict and **disaster**, where a disaster is an outcome that goes against the character. The scene is followed by what he called a **sequel**, in which the character reacts, faces a dilemma and makes a decision. The decision becomes the goal of the next scene, so the two halves chain into a loop.

afterFigure.text: The loop is useful because it explains pacing. A run of scenes without sequels gives the reader no time to feel what happened, and a run of sequels gives them nothing to watch.

workedSteps.text: Start with what the cook is after in the scene, which is smaller than her ambition for the whole story.
Now look at what the owner tells the cook before she answers.
Look for the line where the value changes direction. The owner offers the cook a share of the restaurant in place of a raise.
workedSteps.math: Turning point: the offer of a share

workedSteps.text: Last, say how the scene ends. The cook accepts, and the share also makes her a part-owner of the debts.

steps.headline: A scene begins at +3 on a scale of hope and ends at −2. Measure how far the value moves.

workedSteps.text: Write the start and the end on the scale.
Count from the start down to zero, then from zero to the end.
workedSteps.math: 3 to 0 is 3 points, then 0 to −2 is 2 points

workedSteps.text: The two stretches together make up the whole movement of the value.

lead.text: A character arrives, the characters greet each other, someone makes tea, and only then does the scene begin. The first three lines of the draft in the figure are all of that, and the reader meets the conflict at line 4. The advice, often given as *late in, early out*, is to start the scene at the first line of conflict and to leave it soon after the turn.
Cutting the opening does not remove information, since the reader can assume that Maya arrived and was let in. It removes the delay before the goal, the opposition and the stakes appear.

afterFigure.text: Line 4 gives us Maya's goal, which is to say she is leaving, and line 5 gives us Tom's opposition, in the form of a broken promise.

reveal.text: The strongest opening gives the reader a question to carry, such as why she is angry and what the key means.
Opposition is what turns a goal into a scene. Without it, the goal is simply handed over and no value has anywhere to move.

lessons.orientation: Build a scene around a goal, a conflict and a turning point, and enter and leave it at the right moments.
lessons.nextAction: Write dialogue that carries subtext and gives each speaker a voice.

blocks.text: Here is a scene in full: a cook asks the owner of a restaurant for a raise, the owner says yes, and the cook thanks her and goes back to the kitchen. Every sentence is clear and nothing is wrong with it, yet nobody would remember it a minute later. What would have to be in it for us to care?

“More conflict” is the usual answer, but it is too vague to help when you are staring at a draft. What this scene lacks is a moment where something changes, so that the cook's hope, or her standing with the owner, is different at the end from what it was at the start.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to build a scene around a goal, a conflict and a turning point, and decide where it should start and end.
intro.whyItMatters: A scene that turns carries the reader along, and a scene that does not can usually be cut.

recap.keyIdea: A scene is a unit of change: a character with a goal meets conflict, a value turns, and the outcome is often a new problem.

blocks.text: A scene is made of a goal, a conflict and an outcome, and its turning point is the line where a value such as hope flips from one side of zero to the other. Swain pairs each scene with a sequel, so that the decision the character makes in reaction becomes the next goal. To tighten a draft, start the scene at the first line of conflict and leave soon after the turn.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at what the characters say inside a scene, and at how a line can mean more than its words.

lessons.title: Dialogue

lead.text: Take the woman who wants to tell a friend that his forgetting her birthday hurt. We could write her line as “I'm angry that you forgot my birthday”, and nothing in it needs interpreting. The other version is “You're busy. I understand. Don't worry about it.” Each of those three sentences says the opposite of what she feels, and the reader hears the hurt more clearly for it. We call the meaning that sits under a line, apart from its words, its **subtext**.
Why does this work better? In life people seldom say what they feel outright, because it gives the other person power, or risks a quarrel, or is not yet clear to themselves.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the reader is doing the work of getting from the left column to the right, and that work is the pleasure. When you write subtext you trust the reader with it, and you make sure that the situation gives them enough to do it.

lead.text: Read the same request three ways, as the table gives it. They all want the same thing, and nobody could mistake one for another. Two things do most of the work. The first is **vocabulary**, the words a person reaches for, and the second is **rhythm**, which covers how long their sentences run and where they pause.

It is tempting to think that dialogue should sound like real speech. Real speech is full of repetitions, false starts and fillers, and a page that reproduced them faithfully would be unreadable. Page dialogue keeps a little of that texture, enough to suggest a speaker, and drops the rest.

lead.text: A **tag** such as *he said* or *she asked* tells the reader who is speaking. Most writers keep the tag plain, because *said* is nearly invisible and the reader looks through it to the line. Tags with adverbs, such as *said angrily* and *said bitterly*, tell the reader the feeling in the writer's own voice, and that is exactly what the line itself was supposed to do.

The alternative is a **beat**, a short action placed beside a line, as in “She straightened the cutlery.” and “He looked at the door.” A beat shows us a body doing something while the mouth says something else, and so it is a natural carrier of subtext.

reveal.text: The plain tag keeps attention on the line, and a beat can add the feeling when a line needs it.

lead.text: Look at the line “As you know, Bob, we have been business partners for ten years.” Bob has been there for all ten years, so the line is addressed to the reader and not to him, and we can hear the join. We call dialogue like this an **exposition dump**, and the “As you know, Bob” phrasing has become a name for it.

What works is to make a character want something that the fact serves. If Dara says “Ten years, and the first time I ask for the ledger you act as if I'm accusing you”, the reader learns the same fact, but now it is a weapon in an argument, and Bob has a reason to answer.

steps.headline: Rewrite “As you know, Bob, we have been business partners for ten years” so that the information comes out through conflict.

Give a character a want that those facts serve. Dara wants the ledger, and the years are her argument for being allowed to see it.
workedSteps.math: Dara wants to see the ledger

workedSteps.text: Let the other character resist. Bob treats the request as an accusation.
Write the line so the facts are used and not announced.
workedSteps.math: “Ten years, and the first time I ask for the ledger you act as if I'm accusing you.”

reveal.text: Lines 1 to 4 are greetings and remarks that the reader can assume, so the trimmed dialogue opens on line 5, the first line in which someone wants something.
A line can be informative and still not be a dump, so ask whether the listener could possibly not know it.
Her words say not to worry, and her hurt lives under them. The reader gets there from the situation, and not from the line alone.

lessons.orientation: Write lines that carry subtext, give speakers distinct voices and avoid exposition that both speakers already know.
lessons.nextAction: Choose a point of view, including second person, and say what each can know.

blocks.text: Suppose a woman wants to tell a friend that she is hurt he forgot her birthday. She could say, “I'm angry that you forgot my birthday.” Or she could say, “You're busy. I understand. Don't worry about it.” Most of us feel that the second is both truer and more painful, even though every sentence in it says the opposite of what she feels. How does a line manage that?

It manages it by leaving a gap between what the words say and what the speaker means, and trusting the reader to cross it. Fiction, plays and game scripts all depend on that gap, because a character who says exactly what she feels sounds like someone filling in a form.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write a line whose meaning differs from its words, give two speakers different voices and spot an exposition dump.
intro.whyItMatters: Readers listen for what a character avoids saying, so a draft with subtext holds attention that a plain one loses.

recap.keyIdea: Good dialogue lets a line mean more than its words, gives each speaker a voice of their own and carries information on conflict.

blocks.text: Subtext is the gap between what a line says and what the speaker means, and characters often avoid saying what they feel. Voices differ in vocabulary and rhythm, and a plain *said* or an action beat lets the line carry the feeling. When a character tells another what both already know, the fix is to make the information a weapon in an argument.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks who is telling the story, and what each choice of narrator lets the reader know.

lessons.title: Point of view

lead.text: Picture a house with Tom inside it and a window left open, and ask where the narrator is standing. In **first person** the narrator is Tom, who says “I locked the door”. In **second person** the narrator addresses him, and the sentence becomes “You lock the door”. In **third person** the narrator refers to him as he or by name, and here two positions are worth separating. A **close third** narrator stays at Tom's shoulder and knows what he knows, while an **omniscient** narrator stands above the house and can report what no one inside it knows.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the window is visible from only one of them. That is the practical meaning of point of view: it is a decision about what the narrator is able to say.

reveal.text: “You” puts the character in the reader's place, and that is why second person suits stories that the reader acts out.

lead.text: All four reach Tom's thoughts, but only the omniscient narrator can say that the window is open. The others share his blind spot, and that is a source of effect. First person gives intimacy, since the reader hears from the character directly. Close third gives nearly as much intimacy with a little more freedom in the prose. Second person is intimate in a stranger way, as if the reader were being told what they do. Omniscient gives distance, and with it the possibility of irony and suspense: we know about the window and Tom does not.

afterFigure.text: It also explains a common slip called head-hopping, in which a scene starts at Tom's shoulder and drifts into another character's thoughts. The reader loses track of whose mind they are in. If you want the freedom of omniscient, take it on purpose and keep it steady.

reveal.text: Suspense often comes from this gap, from the reader knowing something that the character does not.

lead.text: Consider “I locked the door once. I'm sure of it. I checked the lock four times to be certain.” The narrator says once and then reports four checks, and we notice. A first-person narrator has no one to correct them, and so the reader has to compare the account against the facts, and the gap between the two is the effect.
In an unreliable narrator the writer holds the voice steady and lets the facts leak around it.

reveal.text: A narrator may be unreliable through lying, through self-deception or through limited knowledge, and the reader notices in each case from the details.

lead.text: It is easy to run the two together, because second person and present tense often turn up together. The grid shows that they are independent.

afterFigure.text: Interactive fiction leans on one cell in particular. “You open the chest” puts the player into the story in second person, and the present tense matches the moment of choosing. That pairing is a convention and not a necessity, though, and a game that wants a more distant narrator can use “you opened” or “Tom opens”.

reveal.text: The test is whether the narrator can stand outside the character's knowledge.

steps.headline: Name the point of view and the tense of a short passage about Mina on the stairs.

workedSteps.text: The passage reads: “Mina counted the stairs, as she always did when she was afraid. At the top she told herself the landing light had simply burned out.” Look first at the pronoun and name used for the one acting. The narrator uses “Mina” and “she”, and never “I” or “you”.
Look at the verb forms.
Now ask what the narrator knows. We learn what Mina tells herself, and nothing about the landing light itself.
Put the two together.
workedSteps.math: Close third person, in the past tense

steps.headline: Name the point of view and the tense of a second passage about Mina on the stairs.

workedSteps.text: The passage reads: “Mina counts the stairs, as she always does when she is afraid. At the top she tells herself the landing light has burned out, and she does not see the man waiting behind the door.” Look first at the pronoun and name used for the one acting. The narrator uses “Mina” and “she”, and never “I” or “you”.
Look at the verb forms. “Counts”, “tells” and “does not see” are all forms for what is happening now.
Now ask what the narrator knows, and compare it with what Mina knows.

reveal.text: The person and the tense can be changed one at a time, so “You opened the chest” is the same person in a different tense.

blocks.text: Here are four sentences about one evening. “I locked the door and slept badly.” “You lock the door and sleep badly.” “Tom locked the door and told himself he was safe.” And “Tom locked the door and told himself he was safe, though he did not know the window was open.” The events are the same in all four, and what changes is who is telling them and how much that teller is in a position to know.

In the English course you met the narrator, the voice that tells a story. Writing one means deciding where that voice stands, inside the character, at their shoulder or above the whole scene, and each position decides what your reader can be told.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the point of view of a passage, say what its narrator can and cannot report, and choose one for an effect.
intro.whyItMatters: Point of view decides what your reader can know, so picking one on purpose is how you plan surprise and suspense.

recap.keyIdea: Point of view is the position a narrator tells from, and it decides what the reader can know and how close they stand to the character.

blocks.text: First person speaks as the character, second person addresses the character as you, close third stays at a character's shoulder and omniscient stands above them all. Each has a different reach, so only the last can report that a window is open when the character does not know it. Person and tense are separate choices, and a narrator becomes unreliable when the details the reader can check do not match the account.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to the sentences themselves, and to how specific detail and revision make a draft say more with less.

lessons.title: Detail, subtext and revision

lead.text: Compare “Dara's kitchen was a mess” with “Three days of plates leaned against the tap.” The first states a conclusion and leaves nothing for the reader to do. The second gives us plates, a tap and a number of days, and we reach the conclusion ourselves; then we go further than the first sentence could, because three days tells us that someone has stopped looking after the place, and perhaps stopped caring. We call a detail that names something particular a **specific detail**, and the extra information it carries is what we mean when we say that it implies.

afterFigure.text: In the second view, the two that state conclusions are marked as telling, and the two that give evidence are marked as showing. A paragraph needs both.

reveal.text: The best detail is often small and a little odd, because that is what makes a reader believe it.

lead.text: “Show, don't tell” is useful advice, and it is also easy to take too far. If every sentence is dramatised, the reader cannot tell what matters, and a story takes four hundred pages to cross a room. **Showing** gives evidence the reader can use to reach a conclusion, as in “She had slept in her coat twice that week.” **Telling** states the conclusion outright, as in “She was exhausted.” Telling is quick, and it suits what the reader only needs to know in passing.

Choose by importance. If Dara's exhaustion drives the scene, show it, and spend the words where the story turns. If it only explains why she is late, tell it in one clause and move on. The same applies to detail in general. More detail is not better, since each unneeded detail dilutes the one that matters.

reveal.text: Evidence invites the reader to work something out, and that small act of inference is much of the pleasure of reading.

lead.text: Most writers want to start a revision by polishing sentences, because sentences are what they can see. The remedy is to work from the largest unit to the smallest, in three passes. In the **structure pass** you read the whole draft for its want, obstacle and change and decide which scenes stay. In the **scene pass** you check each remaining scene for a [[turning point|The line where a value such as hope flips. Met in 'The scene'.]] and for where it should start. In the **line pass** you work sentence by sentence, replacing general statements with specific ones and cutting what does not earn its place.

afterFigure.text: Run them in order and do not skip ahead, even when a clumsy sentence is nagging at you.

reveal.text: The order follows the size of the unit, because each later pass depends on what the earlier ones kept.

lead.text: A common target is a quarter of the draft, so a 1,200-word scene becomes 900. Work out the number before you start, and then cut the least useful passages until you reach it, asking of each one what it gives the reader that nothing else in the scene already gives.
The last check is to **read the draft aloud**. A sentence that makes you take a breath in the middle of a clause is too long, and one where you stumble is usually worded badly.

steps.headline: Revise a draft paragraph about Dara in three passes: structure, scene, then line.

workedSteps.text: The draft reads: “It was late and Dara was very tired. The kitchen was messy. She sat down. She was sad about the news.” In the structure pass, ask whether it serves the story. The news is the story's turn, so the paragraph stays.
In the scene pass, ask where the scene should start. The first sentence tells us the hour and her state before anything happens, so cut it and start on the kitchen.
Next comes the second sentence, “The kitchen was messy”, which states a conclusion and leaves the reader nothing to picture.
Replace “She was sad about the news” with something she does. Then read the paragraph aloud and check the rhythm.
workedSteps.math: Three days of plates leaned against the tap. She stood the letter against the kettle and did not open it.

steps.headline: Cut one fifth from a 200-word passage and count what is left.

workedSteps.text: Find the number of words that go, which is one fifth of 200.
Those 40 words come out of the 200, and the rest of the passage stays.

reveal.text: The same reasoning that orders the passes decides this, since a scene that is rebuilt or cut takes its sentences with it.

lessons.orientation: Replace general statements with specific detail and revise a draft in three passes.

blocks.text: Two sentences describe the same kitchen. The first is “The kitchen was messy.” The second is “Three days of plates leaned against the tap.” The first hands us a conclusion, and the second lets us reach it ourselves and then tells us more: how long, and that someone has given up. What is the second sentence doing that the first cannot?

It gives the reader evidence to reach the verdict for themselves, and a reader trusts what they have worked out more than what they are told. Much of the work of a second draft is finding sentences of the first kind and deciding which to replace with sentences of the second, which to leave alone because they only need saying quickly, and which to cut because they do neither.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to replace a general statement with a specific detail and revise a draft in three passes, structure, scene and line.
intro.whyItMatters: Most of what makes a draft good happens in revision, and an order of work saves you from polishing what you will cut.

recap.keyIdea: Specific detail implies more than a general statement, and revision goes in three passes from the largest unit to the smallest.

blocks.text: A specific detail such as three days of plates gives the reader evidence and lets them reach the conclusion themselves, and showing is worth its words where the story turns. Revise in three passes, structure first, then scene, then line, so that you never polish a sentence that a later cut removes. Put a number on the cut, as with a quarter of 1,200 words, and read the result aloud.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson moves from stories on the page to games, where the player's choices change what a story can do.

lessons.title: Narrative in games

lead.text: A film fixes five events in one order, and every viewer meets them at the same pace. Now look at the same story as a game, where the player can reach the tower through the cellar or over the roof. One route leads past a journal and the other past a guard, so two players finish the game knowing different things. What lets them differ is **agency**, the player's ability to make choices that matter to what happens.

afterFigure.text: Agency is the reason that a game story is not simply a film with interaction. A player can also fail, skip a cutscene, repeat a level or wander off, and the writer has to plan for all of that. So the writer is designing a structure, a set of places and moments, and not a sequence that plays once from start to finish.

diagram.alt: The same story as a film, a fixed row of five events, and as a game, a map with two routes between the gate and the tower. Each player takes one route and sees different information.
diagram.caption: A film fixes the order of events. A game lets each player take a route, so each player meets different parts.

reveal.text: The writer's other tools, such as character and scene, still apply, and agency adds a new constraint on top of them.

lead.text: Where in a game does the story live? Henry Jenkins, in his 2004 essay “Game Design as Narrative Architecture”, offered four answers, which the table gives with an example of each. An **evoked** narrative leans on stories the player already knows, so a game set in a well-known film's world gets the film's story for free. An **embedded** narrative is placed in the game's space for the player to find, as when a journal sits on a shelf. An **enacted** narrative is performed by the player, inside a structure the designer built, as in a stealth level. An **emergent** narrative is a story that arises from play and that no one scripted.

afterFigure.text: They are useful as questions to put to your own design: which of the four is this scene using, and who is doing the telling? A game usually uses several at once, and the kind that suits a moment depends on how much control you want the player to have.

reveal.text: Embedded material is cheap to write and easy to skip, so it often carries detail and not the plot.

lead.text: A game tells you things in two ways. The story says that the hero is gentle, and the mechanics, meaning what the player is able to do and rewarded for doing, may say something else. Suppose the story insists that the hero values every life, but the game gives points and upgrades for defeating every enemy in sight. The player feels the two pulling apart. In 2007 the designer Clint Hocking wrote about this in a blog post on *BioShock*, and the name he gave it, **ludonarrative dissonance**, has stuck.

The word *ludic* means to do with play, so the term joins play and narrative. The lesson for a writer is practical. When the mechanics speak, they speak louder than any dialogue, because the player performs them, and so a story about a gentle hero needs mechanics that let a gentle hero succeed.

reveal.text: The cure lies in the design, by changing what the mechanics reward or what the story claims, since adding more dialogue will not make the clash go away.

lead.text: Don Carson, who had worked on theme park attractions before he worked on games, described in a 2000 article how a designer can tell a story through a space. Look at the room in the figure: a child's bed, a locked door, a stack of chairs against the door, a toy on the floor, from which the player reads that someone shut themselves in with a child and blocked the door from inside. That kind of storytelling is called **environmental storytelling**.

It works because it asks the player to piece the story together, and it fits their freedom, since a player can look at the room for as long as they like or walk straight through it. The cost is that you have no control over how closely it is read.

afterFigure.text: The toy is on the floor, close to the door, and not on the bed, and that single placement tells us where the child last was.

lead.text: A **cutscene** is a stretch of the game in which the player watches and does not play. It lets the writer control timing and the camera, and the price is the player's control. Fifteen two-minute cutscenes come to 30 minutes in which the player can only watch, and some players will skip them, so you should plan for that.

That plan has a simple rule. If a clue matters to what the player does next, put it in at least two places, for instance in a cutscene and also in a line of dialogue or an object in the world. Then a player who skips or misses one of them still gets it.

reveal.text: Sixty out of two hundred is a large group to leave without a clue, and that is the reason for the two-places rule.

steps.headline: Classify the delivery of four pieces of story, using Jenkins's four kinds.

workedSteps.text: Start with a fantasy game that names its hero Arthur and his sword Excalibur and never explains either name.
A journal sits on a shelf in a ruined study and tells part of the backstory. It was written in advance and placed there.
A stealth level has the player sneak past guards, and what happens depends on the player's own actions in a built structure.
A strategy game's war goes badly, and the player tells friends a story about it that no one wrote.

reveal.text: The player carries out the events inside routes and dangers that the designer laid out, which is what makes the narrative enacted.
If the second place is also a cutscene, the same players may skip it, so put it in a different kind of place, such as a line of dialogue or an object in the world.

lessons.orientation: Explain how a player's agency changes what narrative can do, and classify story delivery.
lessons.nextAction: Draw and count the passages of common branching structures.

blocks.text: A film shows us a locked door because the director wants us to see it. A game puts the same locked door in a room and lets the player try the handle, walk past it, or skip the room altogether and take the roof. The story still has to work for a player who does any of those things. How do you tell a story to someone who is free to leave the page?
That freedom changes the writer's job more than any other fact about games.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say how a player's agency changes what narrative can do, and to classify story delivery as evoked, embedded, enacted or emergent.
intro.whyItMatters: A game writer's story has to survive players who skip, fail and wander, so you plan where the story lives before you write it.

recap.keyIdea: Agency makes a game writer design a structure and not a sequence, and the story can reach the player in four different ways.

blocks.text: Because the player can choose, skip and repeat, a game's story is a set of places and moments, and Jenkins's four kinds, evoked, embedded, enacted and emergent, describe how it reaches the player. When the mechanics say something that the story does not, the result is ludonarrative dissonance, and objects and layout can tell a story that no one speaks. Cutscenes take control away, so important information should appear in at least two places.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson draws the structures that let a story branch, and counts what each one costs to write.

lessons.title: Branching structures

lead.text: A passage ends with one binary choice, which is a choice between two options, and so the story has 3 passages and 2 endings. We call each stretch of text the player reads between choices a **passage**, using the word that Twine, a popular tool for writing interactive fiction, uses for it. A structure in which every choice starts new branches that never rejoin is a **tree**.

afterFigure.text: The endings double each time, as 2, 4, 8, and the passages are nearly twice the number of endings, since every ending has the branch passages leading to it. Whoever pays for that is the writer, which is why a first sketch of a branching story and the final game almost never look alike.

reveal.text: Sixteen endings is already more than most teams can write well, which is why designers look for structures that let branches rejoin.

lead.text: Counting only the endings misleads, because every ending has a trail of passages behind it. For three binary choices the levels hold 1, 2, 4 and 8 passages, and the total is 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15. The **writing cost** of a structure is that total, multiplied by the length of an average passage. If each passage runs to 200 words, a tree with 15 passages costs 3,000 words, even though a player will read only four passages in any one playthrough.
The rule is easy to generalise. With three options at each of three decisions, the endings multiply to 3 × 3 × 3 = 27, and the passages, counting the opening, come to 1 + 3 + 9 + 27 = 40.

reveal.text: The player sees five passages in a run of this story and the writer has had to produce thirty-one.

lead.text: The way out of the tree is to let the branches meet again. In the figure's first view, two decisions of three options each make a tree of 13 passages and 9 endings. In the second view, each option still has a passage of its own, and then all three options lead into one shared passage. We call that shared passage a **bottleneck**. With bottlenecks the same two decisions need only 9 passages, and a third decision would add 4 more, where a tree would add 27.

afterFigure.text: It might seem that rejoining makes the choices meaningless, but a choice need not change the ending to matter. Many choices change tone, information or a relationship, and then rejoin, as when one player has the cellar's journal and another has overheard the guard. A later line can acknowledge which it was.

reveal.text: Each decision adds three passages whatever came before, so six of them stay under twenty. A tree with six binary choices would need 127.

lead.text: Sam Kabo Ashwell, in a 2015 survey of the shapes that choice-based games take, names several more structures, and he calls the pure tree a *time cave*. Two of the others are worth drawing. In a **hub**, the player returns to one central passage between strands, and each strand is its own short story, so the cost grows by adding strands and not by multiplying choices. In a **gauntlet**, a main line runs from start to finish and some choices send the player to an early ending, usually a failure, so the main line is the story and the branches are risks.

afterFigure.text: Both structures are affordable because they are shaped. A hub of five strands of 3 passages each costs 16 passages, and the player decides the order.

blocks.text: A story with one choice has three passages: the one that ends in the choice, and one for each of its two outcomes. Give each outcome a choice of its own and the story needs seven passages, and after a third round of choices it needs fifteen. How many passages will it need after four rounds, and how many endings will it have?
The numbers grow faster than almost anyone expects the first time, and that growth is why a branching story rarely ends up in the shape it was sketched in.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to draw a branching tree, count its endings and passages, and choose a structure that fits a writing budget.
intro.whyItMatters: Branching multiplies writing quickly, so a count made before you begin saves you from a story you cannot finish.

recap.keyIdea: In a tree the endings multiply with every choice, so the writing cost is the count of passages, and bottlenecks and hubs keep it affordable.

blocks.text: A tree of four binary choices has 16 endings and 31 passages, and with three options at each of three decisions it has 27 endings and 40 passages. A bottleneck lets the options rejoin, so the same three decisions cost 13 passages, and a hub of five three-passage strands costs 16. When you plan a branching story, count the passages first and choose the shape that fits what you can write.

lessons.title: State and conditions

lead.text: Suppose a player in a dark hall can take a lantern or leave it, and the next passage, the cellar, should read differently in each case. A **variable** is a named value that the story keeps, and with one we need only one cellar. The first choice sets a variable called `has_lantern`, and the cellar passage reads it.

afterFigure.text: A variable like `has_lantern`, which holds only true or false, is called a **flag**. The test the cellar passage makes, `has_lantern` being true or not, is a **condition**, a true-or-false question that chooses between two pieces of text.

lead.text: Ink is a scripting language for interactive stories, made by the studio inkle and documented in its *Writing with Ink* guide. The table shows the six pieces we need. A **knot** is a named section, a choice begins with a star, a divert arrow sends the story to another knot, a tilde line changes a variable, and a condition in curly braces picks between two texts with a vertical bar. The best way to read any script is to keep a running note of each variable's value.

lead.text: A story that remembers has to be tested in every state it can be in, so it is worth counting them. One flag can be true or false, which is 2 states. Two flags give 2 × 2 = 4, and three flags, such as `met_mira`, `has_key` and `saw_fire`, give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, which the figure lists. Each additional flag doubles the count.

That is the reason for a plain rule: only record an event if something later reads it. A flag that nothing tests multiplies the states and changes nothing the reader sees, so it is writing cost with no effect. A variable also needs a starting value, since a flag begins false and a counter begins at zero, and a script that forgets to set it has a state you did not plan.

afterFigure.text: A tree multiplies passages, and flags multiply the states of one passage, so the writing stays modest while the checking grows.

steps.headline: Trace the Mira script when the player chooses “Share your water”.

workedSteps.text: Start with the declaration. `VAR` gives `trust` its starting value.
The player picks the first choice. The tilde line under it adds 2 to `trust`.
The divert moves the story to the gate knot, where the story tests `trust >= 2`.
With `trust` at 2, the condition `2 >= 2` is true, so the text before the bar is shown.

steps.headline: Change the script so that sharing water adds 1, and trace the same choice.

workedSteps.text: Trust starts at the declared value.
Sharing now adds 1 and nothing more.
Next the story reaches the gate, where the condition decides which text is shown.

reveal.text: The same passage and the same condition produce different text, because the variable differs. That is the saving a variable gives over writing two gate passages.

lessons.orientation: Use variables and conditions to make a story remember, and read a short script to say what it will show.
lessons.nextAction: Write barks, quest text and interface strings that work in repeated, interrupted and translated play.

blocks.text: Here is a passage in which a woman called Mira stands at a gate, and whether she unlocks it depends on something the player did two scenes earlier, when she asked them for water. The passage is written once, as a single passage, and yet it behaves as if it knew the player's history. How can a few lines of text know what you did two scenes ago?
They know because the story keeps a note, a value that changes when the player acts and that the passage checks before deciding which sentence to print.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a short ink script and say what it will show, and count the states that a set of flags creates.
intro.whyItMatters: Variables let one passage serve many histories, and counting states tells you how much a story will cost to test.

recap.keyIdea: A variable lets one passage show different text for different histories, and each flag you add doubles the states you have to check.

blocks.text: A variable is a value the story keeps, a flag is a variable that holds only true or false, and a condition is a test that chooses between two texts. Reading an ink script means keeping a running note of each variable and testing the condition when the passage is reached. Three flags give eight states, so record an event only when something later will read it.

lessons.title: Writing game text

lead.text: Think of a combat line such as “Watch your left!”, played whenever an enemy appears on a character's left. The first time it is useful, and by the twentieth it is background noise or a joke. We call a short line spoken in response to a game event a **bark**, and barks are where game text differs most from prose, because a page is read once and a bark is heard again and again.

afterFigure.text: The combat line is triggered every 10 seconds, and in a 6-minute fight that is 360 ÷ 10 = 36 plays. If the game has only one line for that trigger, the player hears it 36 times, which is **repetition**. To avoid any repeat, the game needs 36 distinct lines, and a writer who does not do that sum will find out in testing.

reveal.text: Allowing repeats trades some freshness for writing time, and the right trade depends on how often the player will hear the line.

lead.text: Quest text has two jobs. It has to say what to do, and it has to say why now. Compare “Go to the harbour” with “Take the map to the harbourmaster. The tide turns at noon.” The second names an action, an object, a place and a deadline, and the deadline is what makes the action feel worth taking.

Then test the text against a player who skips every cutscene and reads only the quest log. If it depends on something said in a scene, say it again somewhere the player cannot skip. Anything critical goes in at least two places.

reveal.text: An instruction that depends on something said earlier fails for the player who skipped it, and that is the player who needs it most.

lead.text: A button is a fixed width, and its label has to fit. In the first view of the figure the English label “Save and quit” fits comfortably. The French translation, “Sauvegarder et quitter”, is longer, and it runs past the edge. Translated text commonly runs longer than English, and a rule of thumb is to allow roughly 30 to 35 percent more space. This growth is called **text expansion**.

Two more habits help. Never build a sentence by joining fragments, such as a name, a verb and an object, since other languages put the words in different orders and change them for gender and number. Write whole strings with named slots for the variable parts.

afterFigure.text: The rule of thumb is not exact, and real languages vary, so treat 35 percent as a planning figure. An 80-character string planned at 35 percent comes to 108 characters.

blocks.text: A line that works on a page can fail in a game. “Watch your left!” is a fine thing to hear once, but a combat system that triggers it every 10 seconds will have played it thirty-six times by the end of a six-minute fight. By then the player has stopped hearing it, and some of them are laughing at it.

Most text in a game lives under the same pressure, since it is heard over and over, cut off by the next sound, skipped by a player in a hurry and translated into languages that need more room than English.

intro.whyItMatters: Players hear barks dozens of times and skip scenes freely, so game text has to be planned for repeat, interruption and translation.

recap.keyIdea: Game text has to work when it repeats, when it is cut off, when it is skipped and when it is translated, and each of those can be counted.

blocks.text: A bark played every 15 seconds in a 10-minute fight needs 40 lines to avoid repetition, or 20 if each line may be heard twice, and it should put its key words first in case it is interrupted. Quest text gives an instruction and a reason, and still works for a player who skipped the scenes. Translations run longer, so a 40-character string planned at 35 percent expansion needs room for 54.

lessons.title: Choice, consequence and pacing

lead.text: Look at the two menus. In the first, a thief has been caught, and the player can spare the thief or report the thief. In the second, the menu offers “Say yes” and “Agree”. When the options mean the same, we call it the **illusion of choice**.

afterFigure.text: There are three conditions for what we will call a **meaningful choice**. The options are distinct, so the player has something to weigh. The player can predict something about each, even if not everything, so that the choice is not a coin toss. And the story acknowledges the choice afterwards, so that it was not wasted. The first menu can pass all three, and the second fails the first.

reveal.text: Distinct options do not need to be dramatic. They need to lead to different things.

lead.text: It is tempting to think that hiding the consequences makes a choice more exciting. A little uncertainty does, but a choice with none of the player's knowledge behind it is a coin toss, and players tend to resent it afterwards. If “Spare the thief” might lead to a reward or to a death with no hint of which, the player cannot choose, and can only guess. What a player needs is a reason to expect one outcome over another, even if the expectation turns out to be wrong.

reveal.text: Players tend to forgive a short story with few choices more readily than one with many empty ones.

lead.text: Suppose the player spared the thief. A new branch for every later scene would be ruinous, but a single line can do the work. When the player crosses the market later, the text says, “The thief nods to you from across the market.” A player who reported the thief reads something else, or nothing. We call text that changes to acknowledge an earlier choice **reactive text**, and it uses the flags and conditions from the lesson on state.
The line is also a **delayed consequence**, since it arrives scenes after the choice that caused it. A line of twenty words costs twenty words, where a whole new branch costs a passage.

Planning a small **vignette**, a short scene built around a single choice, starts from a word budget. Take a shared opening of 250 words that every player reads, then three branches of 150 words each, one for each option. The total is 250 + 3 × 150 = 700 words. If the branches then rejoin in a passage of 100 words, that passage is read by everyone and counts once, so the total becomes 800.
The shared opening is read by every player, so it earns its length, and each branch is read by only a third of them, so the budget there should be spent on what makes the options feel different.

afterFigure.text: Pacing follows from the same numbers. If you spread six choices through 2,400 words, there are about 400 words between one choice and the next.
