lessons.nextAction: You can now plan a short branching story, with a structure, state and text that a budget can pay for.

blocks.text: A game offers two menus. The first says “Spare the thief” or “Report the thief”. The second says “Say yes” or “Agree”. You feel the difference straight away, though it is hard to say what it is.

A choice is one of the few things in a game that only the player can do, so the writer's job is to make it worth doing, and that turns out to depend as much on what the player knows before choosing as on what happens afterwards. Honouring a choice also costs words, and a writer who can count that cost can decide how many choices a story can afford and how far apart to put them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to design choices that are distinct, understood and acknowledged, and plan a small branching vignette inside a word budget.
intro.whyItMatters: Choices are what the player does, so they carry the story's weight, and a word budget decides how many you can honour.

recap.keyIdea: A meaningful choice has distinct options, gives the player something to predict and is acknowledged later, and a word budget shows what that costs.

blocks.text: Menus whose options mean the same thing give only the illusion of choice, and options that cannot be predicted at all make a coin toss. A line of reactive text is the cheapest way to acknowledge a choice, and a delayed consequence shows that the story remembered. A vignette with a 250-word opening and three 150-word branches comes to 700 words, or 800 with a rejoining passage, which you can set against the budget before you write.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a plot, in Forster's sense?
hints: Ask of each option whether it reports events, and whether a later event is tied to an earlier one by a cause.
Look for the option in which the second event happens because of the first.
questions.onCorrect: The word *so* joins the playing to the blackout, which makes the second event the result of the first, and events joined by cause are a plot.

misconceptions.feedback: These are two events in order, which makes a story in Forster's sense, but nothing says one caused the other.
That describes a situation and reports no event, so it holds neither a story nor a plot.
Three events in order are still a story in Forster's sense. Nothing joins them by cause, and a longer list does not turn a story into a plot.

choices.label: The pianist arrived, and then the lights went out.
The hall seated four hundred, and the conductor was the pianist's friend.
The lights went out, so the pianist played on from memory.
The pianist arrived, the audience sat down, and the conductor raised his baton.

acceptedIdeas: The lights went out, so the pianist played on from memory.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The lights went out, so the pianist played on from memory.

questions.prompt: A lighthouse keeper wants to reach the mainland for her sister's wedding, but a storm has closed the sea. Which is the obstacle?
hints: The obstacle is what stands between the keeper and what she wants.
One option is the want itself, and one is only the reason she wants it.
questions.onCorrect: The storm is the obstacle, and it is weather, so an obstacle needs no villain.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the want, the thing she is trying to get. The obstacle is what stands in its way.
A story does not need a villain. The storm already blocks the want, and weather can be an obstacle.
The wedding explains why she wants to cross, which raises the stakes, but it does not block her.

choices.label: her sister's wedding
a villain who has not yet appeared
reaching the mainland
the storm that closes the sea

acceptedIdeas: the storm that closes the sea
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: the storm that closes the sea

questions.prompt: In Ana's summary, the closed bridge is which of the three parts: the want, the obstacle or the change?
hints: Ask whether the bridge is what Ana is trying to get, what stands in her way, or a difference between her start and her end.
questions.onCorrect: The bridge blocks Ana from keeping customers, and whatever blocks the want is the obstacle.

misconceptions.feedback: The want is what Ana is trying to get, which is a bakery that stays open. The bridge is what stands in her way.
A change is a difference between the start and the end, and the bridge is closed from early on.

questions.prompt: Tomas ends the story having passed the exam and no longer thinking of himself as someone who cleans up after others. Which of the three parts is that?
hints: One part is what he is trying to get, one is what blocks him, and one is how he differs at the end.
questions.onCorrect: Tomas is different at the end from the man he was at the start, and that difference is the change.

misconceptions.feedback: His want is the clerk's job. This sentence describes how he differs at the end.
His obstacle is the missing diploma. This sentence describes how he differs at the end.

questions.prompt: Six events happen in a row, and each one after the first happens because of the one before it. How many because-links join them?
hints: Count the events that have a cause.
The first event has nothing before it.
Each later event contributes one link.
questions.onCorrect: Each event after the first adds one link, so n events joined in a chain have n minus 1 links.

misconceptions.feedback: The first event has nothing before it to be caused by, so it adds no link.

questions.prompt: A character gets exactly what she wanted and loses her closest friend to get it. Has she changed, in the sense a story needs?

misconceptions.feedback: Getting the want is part of what is different. She also ends without the friend she began with, so her situation at the end is not her situation at the start.

questions.prompt: What is the name for whatever stands between a character and what they want?

questions.prompt: What do we call what a character stands to lose if the want fails?

misconceptions.feedback: The obstacle blocks the want. The question asks for what is lost if the want fails.

questions.prompt: A plot has seven events, and each event after the first happens because of the one before it. How many because-links join them?

questions.prompt: A script runs 120 pages, and act two begins at 25 percent of the way through. On which page does act two begin?

questions.prompt: In Freytag's pyramid, what is the name of the part that comes straight after the climax?

Catastrophe

questions.prompt: On which page of the 96-page script does act two end?

questions.prompt: What is the four-part story form called whose third part is a twist and which does not need conflict between characters?

Flaw

questions.prompt: What do we call the habit or belief that stands between a character and what they need?

questions.prompt: What name is given to a trait that pulls against a character's other traits and makes the character specific?

questions.onCorrect: A shaking hand is evidence, and the reader concludes that she is afraid or nervous without being told.

misconceptions.feedback: Telling states the quality outright, as “She was nervous” would. This sentence gives evidence and leaves the conclusion to the reader.
Showing and telling are about whether a sentence gives evidence or a conclusion, not about adjectives. This one gives evidence.

choices.label: It tells
Neither, because it has no adjective
It shows

questions.prompt: In a three-pass revision, which pass comes first?
hints: Which pass, done too early, risks the most wasted work?
questions.onCorrect: The structure pass decides which scenes stay, so the later passes only work on what will survive.

misconceptions.feedback: Polishing sentences first risks wasted work, since a later pass may cut the scene they sit in.
Fixing a scene is wasted effort if you later decide the story does not need it, so the scene pass waits until you know which scenes stay.

choices.label: The line pass
The structure pass
The scene pass

questions.prompt: A 1,200-word scene is cut by 25 percent. How many words remain?
hints: Find the number of words cut first.
25 percent is a quarter, so divide 1,200 by 4.
Subtract that from 1,200.
questions.onCorrect: A quarter of 1,200 is 300, so cutting 25 percent leaves 900 words.

misconceptions.feedback: 300 is the number of words cut. The question asks how many remain.
Cutting takes words away, so the result is smaller than 1,200.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 25 percent of 1,200 is 300, and 1,200 − 300 = 900 words remain.

questions.prompt: Dara's draft says “The kitchen was messy.” Which pass should replace it with a specific detail?
hints: Which pass works sentence by sentence?
questions.onCorrect: The line pass is where a general statement becomes a specific one, once the scene around it is known to stay.

misconceptions.feedback: The structure pass decides which scenes stay. Choosing a better sentence inside a scene is finer work than that.
The scene pass checks each scene's turn and where it starts. Replacing one sentence with a sharper one is work on the line.

choices.label: The scene pass
The line pass
The structure pass

questions.prompt: A 200-word passage is cut by one fifth. How many words remain?
hints: Find one fifth of 200.
Subtract that from 200.
questions.onCorrect: A fifth of 200 is 40, so cutting it leaves 160 words.

misconceptions.feedback: 40 is the number of words cut. The question asks how many remain.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One fifth of 200 is 40, and 200 − 40 = 160 words remain.

questions.prompt: A draft's middle scene has no turning point, and its sentences also need polishing. Which should you do first?
hints: Work from the largest unit to the smallest.
questions.onCorrect: A scene with no turn needs fixing or cutting first, because polish spent on it may be wasted.

misconceptions.feedback: Sentences in a scene that may be cut are wasted work, so the scene comes first.
More detail dilutes the details that matter, and the problem here is the scene's shape.
Reading aloud helps at the line pass, and the scene problem is larger than a line.

choices.label: add more detail to every line
fix or cut the scene
polish the sentences
read it aloud once more

questions.prompt: A 1,000-word scene is cut by 30 percent. How many words remain?
hints: Find 30 percent of 1,000.
30 percent is 0.3 × 1,000.
Subtract that from 1,000.
questions.onCorrect: Cutting 300 words from 1,000 leaves 700.

misconceptions.feedback: 300 is how many words are cut. The question asks for what remains.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 30 percent of 1,000 is 300, and 1,000 − 300 = 700 words remain.

questions.prompt: What is the revision pass called that comes last and works on sentences and word choice?
hints: It comes after structure and scene.
questions.onCorrect: The line pass is last, because the sentences you polish are then the ones that will stay.

misconceptions.feedback: The structure pass comes first, and it looks at the whole draft.

questions.prompt: What do we call a sentence that states a quality outright, such as “She was exhausted”, in place of dramatising it?
hints: It names a conclusion and gives no evidence.
questions.onCorrect: Telling is fine for what matters little, and showing is worth the extra words where the reader needs to feel the thing.

misconceptions.feedback: Showing gives evidence. The sentence in question gives the conclusion.

questions.prompt: What name is given to the player's ability to make choices that matter to what happens in the game?
hints: It is the same word used of a character who drives the plot.
questions.onCorrect: The writer has to plan for the choices the player may make, since agency means the events are not fixed.

misconceptions.feedback: The word we want names the ability to make choices, and not the choices themselves.

questions.prompt: A player finds a voice recording in a locker that tells part of the backstory. Which kind of narrative is this?
hints: The story information has been placed in the space for the player to find.
questions.onCorrect: The recording is story material set into the world and waiting to be found, which is what embedded means.

misconceptions.feedback: Emergent stories arise from play and were not scripted. A recording was made in advance and placed there.
Enacted stories are performed by the player's own actions. Hearing a recording only requires finding it.
Evoked stories draw on tales the player already knows. This recording tells new backstory.

choices.label: emergent
embedded
enacted
evoked

questions.prompt: A game's story says the hero is desperately poor, but its mechanics let her buy anything she likes from the first hour. What is this conflict called?
hints: The conflict is between what the story says and what the mechanics reward.
The term joins the Latin for play with the word narrative.
questions.onCorrect: The story and the mechanics tell opposite things about the hero, and Hocking named that kind of conflict ludonarrative dissonance in 2007.

misconceptions.feedback: Agency is the player's ability to make choices that matter. It describes what the player can do, and not a clash between story and mechanics.
Embedded narrative is story placed in the world for the player to find. It describes how story is delivered, not a clash between story and mechanics.
Emergent narrative is a story that arises from play without a script. It names a kind of narrative and not a clash between story and mechanics.

choices.label: emergent narrative
embedded narrative
ludonarrative dissonance
agency

questions.prompt: Of 200 players, 30 percent skip a cutscene that carries a key clue. How many players miss the clue?
hints: Find 30 percent of 200.
30 percent is 0.3.
questions.onCorrect: Sixty players miss the clue, which is why important information should appear in at least two places.

misconceptions.feedback: 30 is the percentage. The question asks for a number of the 200 players.
140 players watch the cutscene. The question asks how many skip it.

questions.prompt: A game set in the world of a well-known film leans on stories the player already knows. Which of Jenkins's four kinds is that? Give one word.
hints: The story is called to mind rather than told.
questions.onCorrect: An evoked narrative borrows weight from stories the player has already met.

misconceptions.feedback: Embedded stories are placed in the world to be found. This one is called to mind from outside the game.

questions.prompt: In an escort level, the player guides a wounded soldier across a battlefield whose routes and dangers the designer laid out. Which of Jenkins's four kinds of narrative is that?
hints: The player performs the story's events.
questions.onCorrect: The player performs the events, inside a structure that the designer shaped.

misconceptions.feedback: Emergent stories arise from play and were not scripted. A designed escort level is scripted.
Embedded stories are placed in the world for the player to find. The player does not find an escort, but carries it out.
Evoked stories draw on tales the player already knows. This level tells its story through what the player does.

choices.label: Emergent
Enacted
Embedded
Evoked

questions.prompt: A key clue appears in one cutscene that some players will skip. At least how many places should critical information appear in, so that skipping one does not lose it?
hints: Think about what happens when a player misses the first place.
One place can be missed.
You need a copy somewhere else.
questions.onCorrect: A second copy, for example in a line of dialogue or an object in the world, keeps the clue available to a player who skipped the first.

misconceptions.feedback: A single place can be skipped, and then the clue is lost.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: If one place can be missed, a second is needed, so the minimum is 2 places.

questions.prompt: What do we call telling a story through objects and layout in a space, with no one speaking?
hints: It comes from theme parks, where designers build sets that tell a story as you walk through them.
questions.onCorrect: Don Carson described the technique in 2000 from his experience in theme park design.

misconceptions.feedback: Embedded narrative is one of Jenkins's four kinds. This question asks for the technique of telling through a space.

questions.prompt: What kind of narrative is a story that a player tells about a war that arose in a strategy game, which no writer scripted?
hints: The story arises from the play itself.
questions.onCorrect: Emergent stories come out of the rules and the player's choices and were not written beforehand.

misconceptions.feedback: Enacted stories are performed within a designed structure. This one arises from play and was not scripted.

questions.prompt: A game has 15 cutscenes, and each lasts 2 minutes. How many minutes of cutscene does a player who skips none watch?
hints: Multiply the number of cutscenes by the length of each.
Check the units are minutes.
questions.onCorrect: Thirty minutes is a lot of time with no control, which is why writers weigh each cutscene against the player's wish to act.

misconceptions.feedback: 17 is 15 + 2. The cutscenes repeat, so the lengths multiply.

questions.prompt: A branching tree has 4 binary choices, and no branch rejoins. How many endings does it have?
hints: Each binary choice doubles the number of endings.
Start with 2 after the first choice.
questions.onCorrect: Every choice doubles the endings, so four choices give 2⁴ = 16.

misconceptions.feedback: 8 is the count after three choices. Each further choice doubles it.
4 is the count after two choices. The tree has two more choices.

questions.prompt: The same tree has 4 binary choices and the opening passage. How many passages must be written in all, counting the opening, every branch and every ending?
hints: Count the passages level by level.
The levels hold 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 passages.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: The endings are only 16 of the 31 passages, so the cost is nearly double the number of endings.

misconceptions.feedback: 16 counts only the endings. The passages before them have to be written too.
15 is the total after three choices. The fourth choice adds 16 more.

questions.prompt: A story has 3 decisions with 3 options each. After each decision, every option has one passage of its own and all the options then rejoin. How many unique branch passages are there in total, not counting the rejoining passages?
hints: Count the branch passages for one decision.
One decision has 3 options, each with its own passage.
Multiply by the number of decisions.
questions.onCorrect: The bottleneck keeps the growth linear, so more decisions add 3 passages each, where a tree would multiply them.

misconceptions.feedback: 27 is the number of endings if nothing rejoined. Here the options rejoin after each decision.
12 would count the rejoining passages too. The question asks for the branch passages only.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each decision has 3 option passages, so 3 × 3 = 9 branch passages.

questions.prompt: A hub has six strands, each of 4 passages, plus the hub itself. How many passages are there in all?
hints: Count the passages in the strands first.
Add the hub.
questions.onCorrect: A hub's cost grows with the number of strands, and the player may visit them in any order.

misconceptions.feedback: 24 counts the strands only. The hub is also a passage to write.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6 × 4 = 24 strand passages, plus 1 hub passage, makes 25.

questions.prompt: Three decisions with 3 options each, in a tree where nothing rejoins, have 27 endings. How many passages are there in all, counting the opening passage?
hints: Count each level of the tree.
The levels hold 1, 3, 9 and 27 passages.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: The endings are 27 of 40 passages, and the budget has to cover all of them.

misconceptions.feedback: 27 counts only the endings. The earlier levels have to be written as well.

questions.prompt: A story has an opening passage and four decisions of three options each. Every option has a passage of its own, and the options then rejoin at one shared passage. How many passages are there in all?
hints: Count the passages in one decision and its rejoin.
3 + 1 = 4 per decision.
4 × 4, plus the opening.
questions.onCorrect: Seventeen passages, where a tree with four decisions of three options would need 121, and the player still decides four times.

misconceptions.feedback: 16 leaves out the opening passage.
13 is the total for three decisions. This structure has a fourth, which adds 4 more passages.
121 is the tree, where nothing rejoins. Here the options rejoin, so the count is far lower.

questions.prompt: A team can afford 20 passages and wants three decisions with three options each. Which structure fits the budget?
hints: Compare each structure's total with the budget of 20.
Three options, three decisions.
questions.onCorrect: The bottleneck structure keeps all three decisions and costs 13 passages, which fits inside 20.

misconceptions.feedback: Forty passages is double the budget of 20.
That is bigger still, at 42 passages against a budget of 20.
That fits the budget but drops one of the three decisions the team wanted.

choices.label: a tree where nothing rejoins, with 40 passages
a tree with two extra endings, with 42 passages
a tree of two decisions, with 13 passages and only 9 endings
a bottleneck structure with one passage per option, with 13 passages

acceptedIdeas: a bottleneck structure with one passage per option, with 13 passages
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: a bottleneck structure with one passage per option, with 13 passages

questions.prompt: A story has 3 decision points with 3 options each, and the branches never rejoin. How many different endings are there?
hints: Each decision multiplies the endings by its number of options.
questions.onCorrect: Endings multiply with each decision, so the cost of a tree rises fast.

misconceptions.feedback: 9 is the count after two decisions. The third multiplies it by 3 again.

questions.prompt: What do we call a structure in which the player returns to one central passage between separate strands?
hints: The central passage connects to each strand.
questions.onCorrect: A hub lets the player explore in any order, and its cost grows with the strands, not by multiplication.

misconceptions.feedback: A bottleneck is a passage where branches rejoin. This question asks for the central passage the player keeps returning to.

questions.prompt: A hub has four strands of 5 passages each, plus the hub. How many passages are there in all?
hints: Count the strand passages first.
Add the hub.
questions.onCorrect: Twenty-one passages, and the player visits the strands in whichever order they like.

misconceptions.feedback: 20 counts only the strands. The hub is a passage too.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4 × 5 = 20 strand passages, plus 1 hub passage, makes 21.

questions.prompt: What do we call a shared passage at which several branches rejoin?
hints: It narrows several paths into one.
questions.onCorrect: A bottleneck pulls branches back together, which keeps a story's cost from multiplying.

misconceptions.feedback: A hub is a centre the player returns to. This question is about a passage where branches rejoin.

questions.prompt: A variable that holds only true or false, such as `has_lantern`, is called what? Give one word.
hints: It is a word borrowed from signalling, where something is either raised or not.
questions.onCorrect: A flag records one yes-or-no fact so that a later passage can read it.

misconceptions.feedback: This is a variable, but one that holds only true or false has a more specific name.

questions.prompt:
In this ink script, what does the player see at the gate after choosing “Share your water”?

VAR trust = 0
=== start ===
You meet Mira.
* [Share your water]
    ~ trust = trust + 2
    -> gate
* [Keep walking]
    -> gate
=== gate ===
{ trust >= 2: Mira unlocks the gate. | The gate stays locked. }
-> END
hints: Work out the value of trust after the choice.
Then test `trust >= 2`.
questions.onCorrect: Sharing adds 2, so `trust` is 2, and `2 >= 2` is true, which selects the text before the bar.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the text for a false test. After sharing, `trust` is 2, and `2 >= 2` is true.
The story reaches -> END only after the gate text has been shown.
That line is shown at the start, before the choice. The question asks what appears at the gate.

choices.label: Nothing, because the story ends.
You meet Mira.
Mira unlocks the gate.
The gate stays locked.

questions.prompt: A story starts with `trust = 0`. The player shares water (`trust + 2`), helps carry a pack (`trust + 1`), then argues with Mira (`trust − 2`). What is trust at the end?
hints: Apply the changes in the order they happen.
Take the changes one at a time and note the value after each.
Subtract 2 last.
questions.onCorrect: A variable carries its value from one passage to the next, so the final text reads 1.

misconceptions.feedback: 3 stops before the argument. The last change subtracts 2.
2 is the value after sharing water. Two more changes follow.

questions.prompt: A story tracks 4 independent true-or-false flags. How many combinations of flag values are possible?
hints: Each flag has two possible values.
Multiply the options of each flag.
questions.onCorrect: Every extra flag doubles the number of states, which is why a flag nothing reads is a cost with no benefit.

misconceptions.feedback: 8 is the count for three flags. A fourth doubles it.

questions.prompt: In `{ trust >= 2: Mira unlocks the gate. | The gate stays locked. }`, what is the test `trust >= 2` called? Give one word.
hints: It is the true-or-false part before the colon.
questions.onCorrect: A condition is a test that is true or false, and it chooses between the text before and after the bar.

misconceptions.feedback: The variable is trust. The test that uses it is a different thing.

questions.prompt: Change the script so that sharing water adds 1 instead of 2, and keep the gate test `trust >= 2`. After sharing once, what is `trust`?
hints: Start from the declared value of trust.
Add the new amount once.
Add the new amount to the starting value.
questions.onCorrect: Trust is 1, and `1 >= 2` is false, so the gate would stay locked after one share.

misconceptions.feedback: 2 was the old amount. The new script adds a smaller amount than that.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: trust starts at 0 and gains 1, so it is 1.

questions.prompt:
Using the same script, what does the player see at the gate after choosing “Keep walking”?

VAR trust = 0
=== start ===
You meet Mira.
* [Share your water]
    ~ trust = trust + 2
    -> gate
* [Keep walking]
    -> gate
=== gate ===
{ trust >= 2: Mira unlocks the gate. | The gate stays locked. }
-> END
hints: That choice does not run the `~` line.
trust keeps its declared value.
questions.onCorrect: Trust stays at its declared 0, and `0 >= 2` is false, so the text after the bar is shown.

misconceptions.feedback: That needs trust of at least 2, and walking on leaves it at 0.
That is shown before the choice, not at the gate.
VAR gave trust the value 0 at the start, so it was set.

choices.label: The gate stays locked.
An error, because trust was never set.
Mira unlocks the gate.
You meet Mira.

questions.prompt: A story starts with `trust = 0`. The player shares water (+2), helps with a pack (+1), then shares food (+2), then argues (−2). What is trust at the end?
hints: Apply the changes in order.
Subtract 2.
questions.onCorrect: Trust of 3 clears the gate test `trust >= 2`, so the gate would open.

misconceptions.feedback: 5 is the value before the argument. The last change subtracts 2.

questions.prompt: A story tracks 3 independent true-or-false flags. How many combinations of flag values are possible?
hints: Each flag has two values.
Multiply the options of each flag.
questions.onCorrect: Eight states from three flags, and the count doubles with every flag you add.

misconceptions.feedback: 6 adds 2 + 2 + 2. The flags combine by multiplication.
3 is the number of flags, not the number of combinations.

questions.prompt: What do we call a named value that a story keeps and can change as the player acts?
hints: `trust` and `has_lantern` are examples.
questions.onCorrect: A variable lets one passage show different text for different histories.

misconceptions.feedback: A condition is a test on a named value. This question asks for the value itself.

questions.prompt: Barks play every 15 seconds in a 10-minute fight. How many distinct lines are needed so that none repeats?
hints: Convert the fight to seconds.
10 minutes is 600 seconds.
Divide by the gap between barks.
questions.onCorrect: One bark every 15 seconds for 600 seconds is 40 plays, so 40 distinct lines avoid any repeat.

misconceptions.feedback: 600 is the length in seconds. Divide it by the gap between barks.
10 is the length in minutes. Convert it to seconds first.

questions.prompt: The same fight plays 40 barks, and each line may be heard at most twice. How many distinct lines are needed?
hints: Each line covers two of the plays.
Divide the plays by the plays per line.
questions.onCorrect: Allowing each line to play twice halves the writing, at the price of some repetition.

misconceptions.feedback: 40 is the number of plays. Each line covers two of them.

questions.prompt: Which quest instruction still works if the player skips every cutscene and reads only the quest log?
hints: A good instruction says what to do and why it matters now.
Look for an action, an object, a place and a reason.
questions.onCorrect: It names the action, the object and the place, and the reason gives it urgency, so it works with nothing else seen.

misconceptions.feedback: It names a place and a person but gives no object to carry and no reason to hurry.
A player who skipped the scene does not know what to do, so it fails exactly when it is needed.
It sets a mood but gives no action, so the player still does not know what to do.

choices.label: “The keeper has been waiting for you since the storm.”
“Take the lamp up to the lighthouse. The ship is due at dusk.”
“Go to the lighthouse and talk to the keeper.”
“You know what to do, so go and do it.”

acceptedIdeas: “Take the lamp up to the lighthouse. The ship is due at dusk.”
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “Take the lamp up to the lighthouse. The ship is due at dusk.”

questions.prompt: An English interface string of 40 characters expands by 35 percent when translated. How many characters is the translation?
hints: Find 35 percent of 40.
Add that to the original length.
questions.onCorrect: A translation can run much longer than the English, so build interface space with slack.

misconceptions.feedback: 14 is the extra length. The question asks for the whole translation.
75 adds 35 to 40 as if it were a number of characters. It is a percentage.

questions.prompt: What is a short line spoken by a character in response to a game event, such as an enemy sighting, usually called?
hints: Its name comes from the sound a dog makes.
questions.onCorrect: A bark is short and repeated, so it has to work when heard many times and when cut off.

misconceptions.feedback: A cutscene is a long scripted scene. This question asks about the short line triggered by an event.

questions.prompt: Barks play every 12 seconds in a 6-minute fight. How many distinct lines are needed so that none repeats?
hints: Convert 6 minutes to seconds.
Divide by 12.
questions.onCorrect: Thirty lines, and a shorter gap or a longer fight would raise the number.

misconceptions.feedback: 360 is the length in seconds. Divide it by the gap.
6 is the length in minutes. Convert it first.

questions.prompt: A 20-character label expands by 50 percent when translated. How many characters is the translation?
hints: Find 50 percent of 20.
Half of 20
Add it to 20.
questions.onCorrect: Thirty characters, so the space for the label has to be a half longer than the English needs.

misconceptions.feedback: 10 is the extra length. The question asks for the whole translation.

questions.prompt: A bark plays every 20 seconds in an 8-minute fight. How many distinct lines are needed so that none repeats?
hints: Convert 8 minutes to seconds.
Divide by 20.
questions.onCorrect: Twenty-four lines, and every extra minute of fight adds three more.

misconceptions.feedback: 480 is the length in seconds. Divide it by the gap.
8 is the length in minutes. Convert it first.

questions.prompt: A 60-character English interface string expands by 35 percent when translated. How many characters is the translation?
hints: Find 35 percent of 60.
Add that to 60.
questions.onCorrect: Eighty-one characters, so a field sized for 60 would cut off the translation.

misconceptions.feedback: 21 is the extra length. The question asks for the whole translation.

questions.prompt: What is the growth in length of interface text when it is translated into another language called?
hints: Many languages need more characters than English for the same meaning.
questions.onCorrect: Text expansion is a reason to leave slack in every field and button.

misconceptions.feedback: Repetition is about a line playing again. This question asks about growth in length.

questions.prompt: Which pair of options is the most distinct?
hints: Look for two options that lead to different actions.
Three pairs name the same action in different words.
questions.onCorrect: The two actions have different consequences, so the player has something to weigh.

misconceptions.feedback: These are two words for one action, so the player has nothing to weigh.
Both options go the same way, so they are one option written twice.
These mean the same thing, and a player will notice that quickly.

choices.label: “Burn the letter” / “Deliver the letter”
“Continue” / “Carry on”
“Go left” / “Go to the left”
“Accept” / “Say yes”

questions.prompt: A dialogue menu offers “Open the door” and “Go through the door”, and both lead to exactly the same result. What is this called?
hints: The menu offers several options but only one outcome.
questions.onCorrect: Players notice when options are identical, and it makes the other choices in the story feel suspect too.

misconceptions.feedback: A meaningful choice has options that are distinct, that the player can partly predict and that the story acknowledges. These two options fail the first test.
A coin toss is a choice the player cannot predict at all. Here the player can predict the result perfectly, and it is the same either way.

choices.label: A meaningful choice
The illusion of choice
A coin toss

questions.prompt: A vignette has a 200-word shared opening and three branches of 180 words each. What is its total word count?
hints: Find the words in the three branches first.
Add the opening.
questions.onCorrect: Seven hundred and forty words, and a shared opening is read by every player, so it earns its length.

misconceptions.feedback: 540 is the branches only. The shared opening has to be added.
380 is 200 + 180, which counts only one branch.

questions.prompt: The same vignette gains a 120-word passage in which all three branches rejoin. What is its total word count now?
hints: Start from the total before the rejoining passage.
The earlier total was 740.
Add 120.
questions.onCorrect: The rejoining passage is read by every player, so it counts once, however many branches lead into it.

misconceptions.feedback: 1,100 would count the rejoining passage three times. It is a single passage.
120 is only the rejoining passage.

questions.prompt: A line is added to a later scene: “The thief nods to you from across the market.” What kind of text acknowledges an earlier choice in this cheap way? Give two words.
hints: It reacts to something the player did earlier.
questions.onCorrect: A line of reactive text costs a sentence, where a new branch would cost a passage.

misconceptions.feedback: A new branch costs a whole passage. This line costs one sentence.

questions.prompt: The vignette is 800 words, and the budget is 1,000 words. How many words are left?
hints: Subtract the vignette from the budget.
The remainder is what is left.
questions.onCorrect: Two hundred words could pay for several lines of reactive text elsewhere in the story.

misconceptions.feedback: 1,800 adds the numbers. The budget is a limit to subtract from.

questions.prompt: A 3,000-word story has 5 choices, spaced evenly. How many words come between one choice and the next?
hints: Divide the length by the number of choices.
The result is the average gap.
questions.onCorrect: A choice every 600 words keeps the player acting and still leaves room for the story.

misconceptions.feedback: 5 is the number of choices. The question asks for the gap between them.
3,000 is the whole length. Divide it by the number of choices.

questions.prompt: A vignette has a 250-word shared opening and four branches of 120 words each. What is its total word count?
hints: Find the words in the four branches.
Add the opening.
questions.onCorrect: Four branches cost 480 words, so the opening is about a third of the total.

misconceptions.feedback: 480 is the branches only. Add the opening.
370 adds only one branch to the opening.

questions.prompt: What do we call a choice whose options are distinct, whose effects the player can partly predict and which the story later acknowledges?
hints: It has three conditions, and the name tells you what the player is left with.
questions.onCorrect: A meaningful choice is distinct, understood and acknowledged, and a choice that fails any of the three feels empty.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what a choice feels like when it fails the test. The question asks for the choice that passes.

questions.prompt: What do we call a consequence that shows up some scenes after the choice that caused it?
hints: The effect arrives later than the choice.
questions.onCorrect: A delayed consequence shows the player that the story remembered, and it can be as small as one line.

misconceptions.feedback: Reactive text is the cheap way to show a consequence. This question asks about when it arrives.

questions.prompt: Ana's six events are joined by cause: the bridge fails, the town closes it, the bakery loses customers, Ana buys a cart oven, she bakes at the market, and a queue forms. Suppose the cart oven is cut and the other five events are kept in order. What happens to the plot?
hints: Ask what caused Ana to bake at the market.
A plot needs each event after the first to happen because of the one before.
questions.onCorrect: Each event in a plot leans on the one before it, so removing a cause leaves the next event hanging, which a reader feels as a jump.

misconceptions.feedback: Order is what a story has. A plot needs each event to happen because of the one before, and nothing among the remaining events explains how Ana gets to the market.
The closed bridge explains the lost customers, but not how Ana reaches them again. That step was the cart oven, and without it the chain has a gap.
A chain is only as strong as each link. Removing an event that causes the next one leaves the next one unexplained, however short the chain becomes.

acceptedIdeas: It breaks, because baking at the market would have no cause
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It breaks, because baking at the market would have no cause

choices.label: It breaks, because baking at the market would have no cause
It still holds, because the other five events come in the same order
Nothing changes, because the reader still knows the bridge was closed
It becomes tighter, because a shorter chain is easier to follow

questions.prompt: A draft has six events in time order, and none of them happens because of another. In Forster's terms, what does the writer have?
hints: Forster used one word for events in time order and another for events joined by cause.
questions.onCorrect: Events in order make a story in Forster's sense, and joining them by cause would turn it into a plot.

misconceptions.feedback: A plot needs events joined by cause. These six are only in order, so each one follows the last without being produced by it.
Forster's distinction has nothing to do with how many events there are. It depends only on whether the events are joined by cause or simply follow one another.

choices.label: A story
Neither, because six events are too few
A plot

questions.prompt: A 120-page script moves from act one into act two on page 45, where the 25, 50 and 25 percent convention would put the turn on page 30. What does that tell the writer?
hints: Ask whether the 25, 50 and 25 percent figures are a law or a habit.
A convention tells you where an audience used to the form expects a turn.
questions.onCorrect: A convention tells you what an audience expects, so departing from it is a choice to make knowingly and not a mistake in itself.

misconceptions.feedback: The proportions are a convention that screenwriting teachers pass on, not a law of drama. Plenty of good scripts turn later or earlier than page 30.
The convention does place the turns on pages, which is what makes it useful as a check. It only fails to say that a script must follow it.

acceptedIdeas: The turn is later than audiences expect, which the writer may choose on purpose
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The turn is later than audiences expect, which the writer may choose on purpose

choices.label: The script breaks a rule of drama, so the writer has to restructure it
The turn is later than audiences expect, which the writer may choose on purpose
The convention says nothing here, because a turn cannot be placed on a page number

questions.prompt: In a draft with 8 major events, the protagonist's own decisions bring about 2 of them, and the other 6 happen to her. What does that say about her?
hints: For each event, ask whether her decision brought it about.
questions.onCorrect: Only a quarter of the major events turn on her decisions, so the fix is to give her choices that cause what now merely happens to her.

misconceptions.feedback: Being present is not the test. Agency asks whether the plot turns on her decisions, and six of the eight events would have happened whatever she chose.
A vivid character can still be carried along by events. Agency is about whether her decisions cause what happens, and the count shows that most of them do not.

acceptedIdeas: She has little agency, so for most of the story she is a passenger
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: She has little agency, so for most of the story she is a passenger

choices.label: She has little agency, so for most of the story she is a passenger
Her agency depends on how vivid she is, which the count cannot show
She has plenty of agency, because she is present at every event

questions.prompt: On a scale of hope from −3 (despair) to +3 (confidence), four scenes begin and end at the values below. Which of them has a turning point?
hints: A turning point is where the value changes sign.
questions.onCorrect: Hope crosses zero from +2 to −1, so the value flips, which is what a turning point does.

misconceptions.feedback: Hope rises a little, but it stays on the same side of zero, so the scene ends where it was heading and nothing has turned.
Hope falls further, but it was already below zero. The scene deepens the despair without changing its direction.
The value has not moved at all, so the scene has no turn, however much happens in it.

choices.label: From +2 to +2
From +2 to +3
From +2 to −1
From −1 to −3

questions.prompt: A draft scene has 40 lines. The first 12 are arrival and small talk, and line 13 is the first line of conflict. Where should the scene start?
hints: Late in, early out: where does the scene's conflict begin?
questions.onCorrect: Starting at line 13 loses nothing the reader needs, since they will assume the arrival, and it cuts twelve lines of delay.

misconceptions.feedback: The reader can assume the arrival. Showing it only delays the goal and the opposition by twelve lines.
Half the small talk still holds the reader back from the conflict, and the advice is to enter the scene where the conflict starts.

acceptedIdeas: At line 13, the first line of conflict
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At line 13, the first line of conflict

choices.label: At line 7, halfway through the small talk, so the start is not abrupt
At line 1, so that the reader sees the character arrive
At line 13, the first line of conflict

questions.prompt: A fourth guest asks for the salt: “Er, I don't suppose, if it's no trouble, the salt?” What does most to give that line a voice of its own?
hints: Take out the words that all three speakers share, and look at what is left.
questions.onCorrect: The hedges are vocabulary and rhythm at once, so they tell us the guest is nervous without anyone saying it.

misconceptions.feedback: Every guest at the table makes the same request, so the request cannot be what tells this one apart.
A long line could just as easily sound pompous or calm. This line is long because it is full of hedges, and the hedges are what sound nervous.

acceptedIdeas: The hedges: er, I don't suppose and if it's no trouble
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The hedges: er, I don't suppose and if it's no trouble

choices.label: The request for the salt
The hedges: er, I don't suppose and if it's no trouble
Its length alone, since a long line always sounds nervous

questions.prompt: A dialogue's first 6 lines are greetings and remarks on the weather, and in line 7 one character asks the other for money she is owed. Where should the trimmed dialogue begin?
hints: Begin at the first line in which someone wants something.
questions.onCorrect: Opening on the request puts a want and a likely refusal in front of the reader at once.

misconceptions.feedback: The reader can assume the greeting. Six lines of it only hold back the first line in which anyone wants anything.
The remaining small talk still delays the want, and an abrupt start into a request is what pulls a reader in.

acceptedIdeas: At line 7, where she asks for the money
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At line 7, where she asks for the money

choices.label: At line 4, keeping a little small talk so the start is not abrupt
At line 1, so the reader sees the two of them meet
At line 7, where she asks for the money

questions.prompt: An omniscient narrator tells us that the bridge ahead has been cut, and the rider galloping towards it does not know. What does that give the scene?
hints: Compare what the reader knows with what the rider knows.
questions.onCorrect: The gap between what we know and what the rider knows is what keeps us waiting for the bridge to matter, and it is the main thing omniscience buys.

misconceptions.feedback: An omniscient narrator can reach the rider's thoughts, but close third and first person give us that too. What only this position adds is knowledge that the rider lacks.
That is the effect of head-hopping, which drifts between characters' thoughts. Here the narrator steadily stands above the scene and reports a fact.

acceptedIdeas: Suspense, since we know of a danger that the rider does not
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Suspense, since we know of a danger that the rider does not

choices.label: Closeness, since we hear the rider's thoughts directly
Confusion, since the reader no longer knows whose mind they are in
Suspense, since we know of a danger that the rider does not

questions.prompt: A game's writer wants to address the player as “you”. Which tense does that commit the writer to?
hints: Can you write “you” in the past tense?
questions.onCorrect: Any person can be told in either tense, which is why the grid has six cells and each of them can be used.

misconceptions.feedback: Second person and the present often go together in games, but that is a convention. “You opened the chest” is second person in the past.
Many stories are told in the present, and the choice of tense is separate from the choice of person.

acceptedIdeas: Neither, since person and tense are separate choices
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Neither, since person and tense are separate choices

choices.label: The present, because second person only works in the present
The past, because a story has already happened when it is told
Neither, since person and tense are separate choices

questions.prompt: You have decided to cut a quarter of a 1,200-word scene. Which sentences should you look at first?
hints: Which sentences give the reader nothing they did not already have?
questions.onCorrect: A telling sentence that repeats what the evidence already showed costs words and adds nothing, so it is usually the cheapest thing to lose.

misconceptions.feedback: An even cut treats every sentence as equally useful. Some paragraphs carry the turn, and the cut should fall on the least useful passages wherever they are.
The specific details are what let the reader reach the conclusion, so they are usually the last thing to cut.

acceptedIdeas: The ones that tell what the showing sentences have already made clear
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ones that tell what the showing sentences have already made clear

choices.label: The specific details, since they take the most words
The ones that tell what the showing sentences have already made clear
An even share from every paragraph, so the scene keeps its shape

questions.prompt: What does reading a draft aloud catch that reading it silently tends to miss?
hints: Think about what your ear notices that your eye skips over.
questions.onCorrect: The ear catches rhythm the eye misses, which is why reading aloud belongs in the line pass.

misconceptions.feedback: A missing turn is a problem of the scene, which the scene pass finds by asking where the value changes, not by listening.
Spelling is easier to see than to hear, since a misspelt word usually sounds right when you say it.

acceptedIdeas: Sentences that make you stumble or run out of breath
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sentences that make you stumble or run out of breath

choices.label: Scenes whose turning point is missing or late
Spelling mistakes and typing slips
Sentences that make you stumble or run out of breath

questions.prompt: Of 200 players, 30 percent skip a cutscene that carries a clue they need for the next puzzle. What should the writer do?
hints: How can a player who skips the cutscene still meet the clue?
questions.onCorrect: A clue that matters to what the player does next belongs in at least two places, so missing one of them costs nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes control away from all 200 players to reach the 60 who skip, and a player who is forced to watch can still look away.
Sixty players would reach the puzzle without what they need to solve it, which is a large number of people to leave stuck.

acceptedIdeas: Repeat the clue in a line of dialogue or an object in the world
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Repeat the clue in a line of dialogue or an object in the world

choices.label: Repeat the clue in a line of dialogue or an object in the world
Make the cutscene impossible to skip, so that everyone sees the clue
Leave it as it is, since most players still see the clue

questions.prompt: Which of these pieces of story should appear in at least two places in a game?
hints: Which of these would stop a player if they missed it?
questions.onCorrect: Information the player needs in order to act is critical, so it gets a second place, while atmosphere can live in one.

misconceptions.feedback: The curtains are atmosphere, and a player who misses them can still do everything the game asks. One place is enough for them.
Nothing the player has to do depends on the rumour, so it can live in one place, and a player who misses it loses only colour.

acceptedIdeas: The code to the vault door the player must open next
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The code to the vault door the player must open next

choices.label: The colour of the curtains in the governor's study
A rumour that adds to the mood but changes nothing the player does
The code to the vault door the player must open next

questions.prompt: What does a cutscene give the writer, and what does it cost?
hints: Who is in control while a cutscene plays?
questions.onCorrect: The writer decides exactly what is seen and when, and the player can only watch, which is the trade every cutscene makes.

misconceptions.feedback: A cutscene works the other way round. The player watches and does not play, so the writer gains control and the player loses it.
Some players skip cutscenes, which is why critical information should also appear somewhere else.

acceptedIdeas: It gives control of timing and camera, at the cost of the player's control
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It gives control of timing and camera, at the cost of the player's control

choices.label: It gives control of timing and camera, at the cost of the player's control
It gives a guaranteed audience, at no cost, since players watch every cutscene
It gives the player agency, at the cost of the writer's control

questions.prompt: Why is the closed bridge the obstacle in Ana's summary?
hints: Think about what Ana is trying to get, and what the bridge does to that.

acceptedIdeas: It stands between Ana and the customers her bakery needs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It stands between Ana and the customers her bakery needs

questions.onCorrect: The bridge blocks Ana from keeping customers, and whatever blocks the want is the obstacle.

choices.label: It stands between Ana and the customers her bakery needs
It is what Ana stands to lose if the bakery closes
It is a difference between how Ana starts and how she ends

misconceptions.feedback: That describes the stakes, which is what Ana loses if she fails. The bridge is something she meets on the way to what she wants.
A change is a difference between the start and the end, and the bridge is closed from early on, long before the end.

questions.prompt: Tomas, a night cleaner, wants a clerk's job at the bank, which hires only people with a diploma. At forty he passes the exam, and by the end he no longer thinks of himself as someone who cleans up after others. Which of these sentences is the change in Tomas's summary?
hints: Ask which sentence describes a difference between the start of his story and its end.

acceptedIdeas: Change: Tomas has a diploma and no longer sees himself as a cleaner.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Change: Tomas has a diploma and no longer sees himself as a cleaner.

questions.onCorrect: Tomas is different at the end from the man he was at the start, and that difference is the change.

choices.label: Change: Tomas sits an exam when he is forty years old.
Change: Tomas still wants a clerk's job at the bank.
Change: the bank hires only people who hold a diploma.
Change: Tomas has a diploma and no longer sees himself as a cleaner.

misconceptions.feedback: That is something Tomas does on the way. A change is a difference between his situation or belief at the start and at the end.
That is his want, and it is the same at the start and at the end. A change has to be a difference.
That is the obstacle, which blocks him. It is not a difference between how his story starts and how it ends.

questions.prompt: Ruth, a surgeon, wants to head her department. She never learned the patience to listen to patients, and she believes that listening wastes time. Which of these is her flaw?
hints: A flaw is the belief or habit that stands between the want and the need.

acceptedIdeas: Her belief that listening wastes time
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Her belief that listening wastes time

questions.onCorrect: The belief that listening wastes time keeps her from the patience she lacks, so it is the flaw standing between her want and her need.

choices.label: Her belief that listening wastes time
Her wish to head the department
Her missing patience for listening

misconceptions.feedback: That is what she is chasing, which makes it her want and not her flaw.
That is what she lacks to be whole, which makes it her need and not her flaw.

questions.prompt: A dialogue draft opens with five lines. Line 1 is “Morning.” Line 2 is “Cold, isn't it?” Line 3 is “Bitter. Mind the step.” Line 4 is “Thanks.” Line 5 is “Forty pounds, Ben, and you said Friday.” Where should the trimmed dialogue begin?
hints: Begin at the first line in which someone wants something.

acceptedIdeas: At line 5, where Ben is asked for the money
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At line 5, where Ben is asked for the money

questions.onCorrect: Opening on the demand puts a want and a likely refusal in front of the reader at once.

choices.label: At line 1, so the reader sees the two of them meet
At line 3, keeping some small talk so the start is not abrupt
At line 5, where Ben is asked for the money

misconceptions.feedback: The reader can assume the greeting. Four lines of it only hold back the first line in which anyone wants anything.
The remaining small talk still delays the want, and an abrupt start into a request is what pulls a reader in.

questions.prompt: Mina counts the stairs, and the narrator mentions a man behind the door whom she does not see. Which kind of third-person narrator tells this passage?
hints: Compare what Mina notices with what the narrator reports.

acceptedIdeas: An omniscient narrator, who knows more than Mina does
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An omniscient narrator, who knows more than Mina does

questions.onCorrect: The narrator reports the man behind the door, whom Mina has not seen, so this narrator stands above the scene.

choices.label: A close third narrator, who knows only what Mina knows
An omniscient narrator, who knows more than Mina does

misconceptions.feedback: A close third narrator stays at Mina's shoulder and cannot report a man she has not seen, so this narrator knows more than she does.

questions.prompt: Most players know the legend those names come from. Which of Jenkins's four kinds of narrative is that?
hints: The story is called to mind, not told.
questions.onCorrect: An evoked narrative borrows weight from stories the player has already met.

choices.label: Embedded
Emergent
Evoked
Enacted

misconceptions.feedback: Embedded stories are placed in the game's space to be found, such as a journal on a shelf. These names call up a story from outside the game.
Emergent stories arise from play and were never scripted. These names were chosen by the designer.
Enacted stories are performed by the player inside a structure the designer built. Here the player only recognises the names.

questions.prompt: Two players of a board game form an alliance, break it and retell the betrayal for years, though no writer scripted any of it. Which of Jenkins's four kinds of narrative is that, in one word?
hints: The story arises from the play itself.
questions.onCorrect: Emergent stories come out of the rules and the players' choices and were not written beforehand.

misconceptions.feedback: Enacted stories are performed by the player inside a structure the designer built. This one arose from play and no one planned it.
Embedded stories are placed in the game for the player to find. Nobody placed this one.

questions.prompt: A story has an opening passage and then 6 decisions with 2 options each. Each option has a passage of its own, and the two options then rejoin at one shared passage. How many passages are there in all?
hints: Count the passages that one decision needs.
One decision has 2 option passages and 1 rejoining passage.
Multiply by the number of decisions, then add the opening.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each decision needs 2 option passages and 1 rejoining passage, which is 3, so 6 × 3 = 18, and the opening passage makes 19.

questions.onCorrect: Each decision adds only 3 passages, so six decisions cost 19, where a tree with six binary choices would need 127.

misconceptions.feedback: 18 leaves out the opening passage, which also has to be written.
13 counts the option passages and the opening but leaves out the passage where the options rejoin after each decision.
127 is the tree, where nothing rejoins. Here the options rejoin after every decision, so the count is far lower.

questions.prompt: Why does the bottleneck structure need so many fewer passages than the tree?
hints: Compare what happens after the options in the two structures.

acceptedIdeas: The options rejoin, so later passages are written once, not once per route
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The options rejoin, so later passages are written once, not once per route

questions.onCorrect: Because the options rejoin, each later passage is written once however many routes lead into it, which keeps the cost from multiplying.

choices.label: The options rejoin, so later passages are written once, not once per route
It has fewer decisions, so the player has fewer choices to make
Each option has a shorter passage, so each one costs fewer words
It has fewer options at each decision, so there are fewer branches

misconceptions.feedback: Both structures have the same three decisions. The saving comes from how the paths meet, not from dropping a decision.
The count is of passages, not words, and each option still has a passage of its own. The saving comes from somewhere else.
Both structures give every decision three options. The difference is in what happens after the options.

questions.prompt: A story has 3 decision points with 4 options each, and the branches never rejoin. How many different endings are there?
hints: Each decision multiplies the endings by its number of options.
After the first decision there are 4 endings.
Multiply by 4 again for each further decision.
questions.onCorrect: Endings multiply with each decision, so three decisions of four options already give 64 endings.

misconceptions.feedback: 12 is the number of decisions times the number of options. Each decision multiplies the endings by its options instead.
16 is the count after two decisions. The third decision multiplies it by 4 again.

questions.prompt: After sharing the water, `trust` holds 2. Is the test `trust >= 2` true or false?
hints: Read `>=` as 'greater than or equal to'.
questions.onCorrect: With `trust` at 2, the test `2 >= 2` passes, because the two sides are equal.

choices.label: True, because 2 is at least 2
False, because 2 does not exceed 2

misconceptions.feedback: `>=` means greater than or equal to, so a value equal to 2 passes the test. Only a value below 2 fails it.

questions.prompt: Sharing once now leaves `trust` at 1, and the gate still tests `trust >= 2`. Which text does the player see at the gate?
hints: Put the value of `trust` into the test.
questions.onCorrect: Trust is 1, and `1 >= 2` is false, so the text after the bar is shown and the gate stays locked.

choices.label: Mira unlocks the gate.
The gate stays locked.

misconceptions.feedback: That text is shown only when `trust >= 2` is true, and 1 is below 2.

questions.prompt: A story tracks 5 independent true-or-false flags. How many combinations of flag values are possible?
hints: Each flag has two values.
Each flag doubles the number of combinations.
Multiply 2 by itself once for each flag.
questions.onCorrect: Thirty-two states from five flags, and the count doubles with every flag you add.

misconceptions.feedback: 10 adds 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2. The flags combine by multiplication, so each one doubles the count.
16 is the count for four flags. A fifth flag doubles it.
25 is 5 × 5. Each flag has two values, so each one doubles the count.

questions.prompt: Why does dividing 600 seconds by 15 seconds give the number of distinct lines needed?
hints: Think about what the 15 seconds measures, and how many of them fit into the fight.

acceptedIdeas: A bark plays once every 15 seconds, so the number of gaps is the number of plays
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bark plays once every 15 seconds, so the number of gaps is the number of plays

questions.onCorrect: One bark plays in each 15-second gap, so the 40 gaps in the fight are 40 plays, and each play needs a different line to avoid repeating.

choices.label: Division turns the length of the fight from seconds into minutes
A bark plays once every 15 seconds, so the number of gaps is the number of plays
Each line must fill 15 seconds, so 15 seconds is how much to write

misconceptions.feedback: Dividing seconds by seconds gives a count, not a new unit. The 40 is a number of plays.
The 15 seconds is the gap between barks, not the length of a line. A bark is short, and the gap says how often one plays.

questions.prompt: In a later scene a stallholder says, “They tell me you went easy on that thief,” a line that only a player who spared the thief reads. What kind of text is that?
hints: It reacts to something the player did earlier.
questions.onCorrect: A line of reactive text costs a sentence, where a new branch would cost a passage.

choices.label: Reactive text
A new branch
A shared opening

misconceptions.feedback: A new branch is a whole passage of its own. This is a single line inside a scene that every player reads.
A shared opening is read by every player before the choice. This line comes later and only some players see it.

flashcards.front: State the want, the obstacle and the change of a story you know, in three sentences. How sure are you that each part is present?
flashcards.back: A story you can summarise in those three sentences has a direction, a cost and an ending that differs from its start.

flashcards.front: In Forster's sense, what turns a story into a plot?
flashcards.back: A plot joins its events by cause, so each one happens because of the one before it, where a story only puts them in time order.

flashcards.front: What do we call what a character stands to lose if the want fails?
flashcards.back: The stakes are the cost of failure, and they make us care about the outcome.

flashcards.front: In Freytag's pyramid, which part sits at the top?
flashcards.back: The climax is the turning point in the middle of the pyramid, and falling action and catastrophe still follow it.

flashcards.front: A script is 200 pages long. On which page does act one end, at 25 percent?
flashcards.back: A quarter of 200 pages is page 50.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A quarter of 200 pages is page 50.

flashcards.front: Take a story you know and try to place it in three acts and in kishotenketsu. How well does each fit?
flashcards.back: Each structure describes one common pattern, so a story can fit one well and another badly without being worse for it.

flashcards.front: Why is 'Mara went back for the dog while the roof was coming down' better characterisation than 'Mara is brave'?
flashcards.back: A costly choice is evidence we can watch, while a trait only asks us to take the writer's word for it.

flashcards.front: What do we call a character's ability to make decisions that drive events?
flashcards.back: Agency means the plot turns on what the character decides, so a rescue from outside would remove it.

flashcards.front: Write a want, a need and a flaw for a character, then one costly choice. How clearly does the choice show the flaw?
flashcards.back: A choice shows a flaw when keeping the flaw is the easier option and costs something.

flashcards.front: A scene is built from a goal, a conflict and what third part, which says how it ends?
flashcards.back: A scene has a goal, a conflict and an outcome, and it changes something.

flashcards.front: What does the advice 'late in, early out' mean for a draft scene?
flashcards.back: Start the scene at the first line of conflict and end it soon after the turn, so arrival and small talk stay outside.

flashcards.front: Write one page: a scene with a goal, a conflict and a turning point. Rate each as clear or not.
flashcards.back: A scene is complete when its goal meets opposition and the value turns, so check each of the three.

flashcards.front: What do we call the gap between what a character says and what they mean?
flashcards.back: Subtext is the meaning under a line, and it lets people say one thing while meaning another.

flashcards.front: Why is 'said' usually a better tag than 'said angrily'?
flashcards.back: The line itself should carry the feeling, and a plain tag lets the reader look through it.

flashcards.front: Write one line asking for a lift to the airport in three characters' voices. How different do they sound?
flashcards.back: Voices differ in vocabulary and rhythm, so check both in your three versions.

flashcards.front: A third-person narrator who can report what no character knows is called what?
flashcards.back: An omniscient narrator stands outside every character, so it can report what none of them knows.

flashcards.front: Why can a first-person narrator be wrong?
flashcards.back: A first-person narrator knows only what they know, and may also misreport it, so the reader has to check the account against the facts.

flashcards.front: Tell one event in two points of view. What does each version know that the other cannot?
flashcards.back: Each position decides what the narrator can report and how close the reader stands to the character.

flashcards.front: Is 'She was exhausted' showing or telling?
flashcards.back: It is telling, because it states a quality outright, and a showing sentence would give evidence such as sleeping in her coat.

flashcards.front: A 1,200-word scene is cut by a quarter. How many words are left?
flashcards.back: A quarter of 1,200 is 300, so 900 words are left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A quarter of 1,200 is 300, so 900 words are left.

flashcards.front: Revise 200 words of your own: cut one fifth and replace one general statement with a specific detail. How much clearer is it?
flashcards.back: A fifth of 200 words is 40, which leaves 160, and a specific detail often replaces several vague words.

flashcards.front: What is the player's ability to make choices that matter to a game's events called?
flashcards.back: Agency means the writer must plan a structure the player can move through, and not a fixed sequence.

flashcards.front: A game's story says the hero values life, but its mechanics reward killing everything. Name the conflict.
flashcards.back: Ludonarrative dissonance is a conflict between what the story says and what the mechanics reward.

flashcards.front: Why is a game writer's job a structure and not a sequence?
flashcards.back: The player can fail, skip, repeat and act, so the writer designs what happens across many possible runs.

flashcards.front: A tree with 4 binary choices has 16 endings. How many passages does it have in all?
flashcards.back: The levels hold 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 passages, which add to 31.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The levels hold 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 passages, which add to 31.

flashcards.front: What do we call a passage where several branches rejoin?
flashcards.back: A bottleneck pulls the branches back into one passage, so the writing grows by addition and not multiplication.

flashcards.front: Why does counting only the endings underestimate a branching story's cost?
flashcards.back: Every passage between the opening and the endings has to be written too, and there are more of those than endings.

flashcards.front: What do we call a variable that holds only true or false?
flashcards.back: A flag records one yes-or-no fact, such as whether the player took the lantern.

flashcards.front: Three independent flags give how many combinations?
flashcards.back: Each flag doubles the count, so 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each flag doubles the count, so 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.

flashcards.front: Why should a flag only be created for an event that something later will read?
flashcards.back: A flag nothing reads multiplies the possible states and adds writing cost without changing what the reader sees.

flashcards.front: Barks play every 15 seconds in a 10-minute fight. How many distinct lines avoid any repeat?
flashcards.back: 600 seconds divided by 15 is 40 lines.

flashcards.front: Where should the key information go in a bark that may be interrupted?
