essays.title: The locksmith's story in three sentences
essays.prompt:
Turn the premise below into the bones of a story. Write one sentence for Marit's want, one for the obstacle and one for the change, add a sentence on what she stands to lose, and then list four events of the story so that each one causes the next.

The premise is invented, and you will work on it in every task of this course. Marit Dahl has been the only locksmith in a harbour town for twenty years, and she has one rule: no proof of address, no door. On a night when a storm has cut the power, a man she has never met asks her to open a flat on Tide Street. He says it was his mother's, that she died on Tuesday, and that the landlord will clear it at eight in the morning. He has no key and no proof.

The premise leaves the rest to you: why she might open the door, what is in the flat, and how the night ends.
essays.expectedScope: Four sentences and a chain of four events: 80 to 140 words. Allow about 10 minutes.
successCriteria: The want is something Marit is trying to get in this story, and it is more than a mood or a trait.
The obstacle stands between her and that want, so that getting it costs her effort.
Says what she loses if she fails.
The change is a difference between her situation or her belief at the start and at the end.
Each of the four events could be joined to the one before it by "so" and not only by "then".

essays.title: The story outlined in five parts
essays.prompt:
Outline the locksmith's story in Freytag's five parts, with one or two sentences for each. Then say in two or three sentences how you would arrange the same material as kishotenketsu, and what the story would gain or lose.

The premise is the one this course's tasks share, and it is invented. Marit Dahl has been the only locksmith in a harbour town for twenty years, and she has one rule: no proof of address, no door. On a night when a storm has cut the power, a man she has never met asks her to open a flat on Tide Street. He says it was his mother's, that she died on Tuesday, and that the landlord will clear it at eight in the morning. He has no key and no proof.

Build on the want, obstacle and change you wrote in the last lesson's task. If you skipped it, use these: Marit wants to help the man without breaking the rule that has kept her licence for twenty years. He has no proof, and the flat will be cleared at eight. By morning she has opened the door, and she no longer believes that the rule was ever about the law.
essays.expectedScope: Five labelled parts and a short comparison: 120 to 200 words. Allow about 12 minutes.
successCriteria: Gives all five parts in order, and each holds events that belong to that part.
The climax is a turning point for Marit, with the events before it leading up to it by cause.
The last part shows the change, so that the ending differs from the beginning.
The kishotenketsu version names its four parts and says what its twist would be.
Says one thing the second shape would gain or lose compared with the first.

essays.title: A character sheet and a costly choice
essays.prompt:
Write a short character sheet for Marit, with a line each for her want, her need, her flaw and one contradiction. Then write the moment in which she makes the choice that shows who she is.

The premise is the one this course's tasks share, and it is invented. Marit Dahl has been the only locksmith in a harbour town for twenty years, and she has one rule: no proof of address, no door. On a night when a storm has cut the power, a man she has never met asks her to open a flat on Tide Street. He says it was his mother's, that she died on Tuesday, and that the landlord will clear it at eight in the morning. He has no key and no proof.

You may keep the want you gave her in the earlier tasks or change it now. Decide the rest yourself. The moment can come from anywhere in the night: on the doorstep, at the lock, or inside the flat.
essays.expectedScope: Four lines and a passage of 80 to 130 words. Allow about 15 minutes.
successCriteria: The need is something she lacks and does not see, and it differs from the want.
The flaw is what keeps her from the need.
The contradiction is a trait that pulls against her others.
In the passage she chooses between two things she values, and the choice costs her one of them.
The passage shows her deciding, and nothing in it decides for her.

essays.title: The scene at the door
essays.prompt:
Write the scene in which the man asks Marit to open the flat. Give it a goal, a conflict, a turning point and an outcome. Under the scene, name the value it turns on and give its sign at the start and at the end.

The premise is the one this course's tasks share, and it is invented. Marit Dahl has been the only locksmith in a harbour town for twenty years, and she has one rule: no proof of address, no door. On a night when a storm has cut the power, a man she has never met asks her to open a flat on Tide Street. He says it was his mother's, that she died on Tuesday, and that the landlord will clear it at eight in the morning. He has no key and no proof.

Write it from Marit's side or from his. You know what she wants from the earlier tasks, or you can take this: she wants to go home with her rule unbroken, and some part of her wants to be talked out of it.
essays.expectedScope: A scene of 150 to 250 words and one line on its value. Allow about 15 minutes.
successCriteria: One character is after something particular in this scene, and the other stands in the way.
The scene opens at or just before the first line of conflict, without arrivals or greetings.
There is a line where the value changes sign, and the scene ends soon after it.
The outcome leaves the character with a new problem or a decision to make.
The line under the scene names one value and gives two signs that match what happens.

essays.title: A conversation rewritten with subtext
essays.prompt:
Rewrite the conversation below. Let the two speakers hide what they feel, give each a voice of their own, replace the adverbs with plain tags or beats, and let the facts come out because someone wants something.

The premise is the one this course's tasks share, and it is invented. Marit Dahl has been the only locksmith in a harbour town for twenty years, and she has one rule: no proof of address, no door. On a night when a storm has cut the power, a man she has never met asks her to open a flat on Tide Street. He says it was his mother's, that she died on Tuesday, and that the landlord will clear it at eight in the morning. He has no key and no proof.

This draft was written badly on purpose.

"Hello," said the man politely. "As you know, you are the only locksmith in this town, and the power has been out since the storm began at six."

"Yes," said Marit tiredly. "I am very suspicious of you, because you have no proof that the flat is your mother's."

"I am sad and desperate," he said sadly. "My mother died on Tuesday and the landlord will clear the flat at eight in the morning, and I want her letters."

"I feel sorry for you, but I am afraid of losing my licence," she said nervously.
essays.expectedScope: A conversation of 120 to 200 words. Allow about 12 minutes.
successCriteria: Neither speaker names their own feeling, and a reader can still tell what each one feels.
The two could be told apart with the tags removed, by their words or the length of their sentences.
Tags are plain, and at least one line is attributed by an action in place of a tag.
The death, the deadline and the letters reach the reader through what a speaker wants and not as an announcement.
Nothing is said only because the reader needs to hear it.

essays.title: One moment from two other points of view
essays.prompt:
Rewrite the passage below twice. First tell it in the first person as the man, who is hiding something. Then tell it in the second person and the present tense, as a text game would address its player. Finish with a sentence on what each of your versions can no longer tell the reader.

The premise is the one this course's tasks share, and it is invented. Marit Dahl has been the only locksmith in a harbour town for twenty years, and she has one rule: no proof of address, no door. On a night when a storm has cut the power, a man she has never met asks her to open a flat on Tide Street. He says it was his mother's, that she died on Tuesday, and that the landlord will clear it at eight in the morning. He has no key and no proof.

The passage was written for this exercise, in close third person and the past tense.

Marit kept the torch on his hands and off his face. They were clean, with a pale band where a ring had been. He said the flat was his mother's, and she noticed that he did not look up at its window. Behind her the van's engine ticked as it cooled. Twenty years, and she had never once opened a door on a stranger's word.
essays.expectedScope: Two versions of 50 to 90 words each and a closing sentence. Allow about 12 minutes.
successCriteria: The first version stays in the first person and reports only what the man could see, hear or think.
In the first version there is a gap between what the man claims and what he lets slip, and the reader is left to notice it.
The second version is in the second person and the present tense from its first verb to its last.
Both versions keep the events of the original and add no new ones.
The closing sentence names something the original could tell that each new version cannot.

essays.title: A paragraph revised in passes and cut by a quarter
essays.prompt:
Revise the paragraph below. It has 113 words, and your version should have 84 or fewer, which is a cut of a quarter. Replace at least two of its stated conclusions with a detail the reader can draw the conclusion from. Under your version, list your changes in the order you made them.

The premise is the one this course's tasks share, and it is invented. Marit Dahl has been the only locksmith in a harbour town for twenty years, and she has one rule: no proof of address, no door. On a night when a storm has cut the power, a man she has never met asks her to open a flat on Tide Street. He says it was his mother's, that she died on Tuesday, and that the landlord will clear it at eight in the morning. He has no key and no proof.

The paragraph comes from an invented first draft, at the point where Marit has opened the door.

The flat was very untidy and it was obvious that nobody had been taking care of it for quite some time. Marit felt extremely uneasy as she walked slowly inside. The man was clearly upset. He went quickly over to the desk and started looking through the drawers in a hurried and anxious way, and it seemed to her that he knew exactly where to look, which was strange. There were a lot of old things everywhere that had belonged to an old woman. It was cold. Marit thought about her licence and about the rule, and she began to realise that she had perhaps made a serious mistake in coming here tonight.
essays.expectedScope: A paragraph of 84 words or fewer and a short list of changes. Allow about 12 minutes.
successCriteria: The revised paragraph is 84 words or fewer.
At least two conclusions that the draft states are replaced by something a person in the room could see, hear or touch.
The man still goes to the desk as if he knows it, and Marit still doubts her decision.
At least one plain statement is kept where a quick fact serves the reader better than a picture.
The list puts changes to what the paragraph does ahead of changes to single words.

essays.title: The flat as a room the player reads
essays.prompt:
Design the mother's flat as a room that tells its story without a narrator. List four to six things the player finds there and where each one is, and then say what a player should be able to work out from them. Finish by naming which of Jenkins's four kinds of narrative this is, and the one clue the player must meet during play.

From this lesson on, the tasks turn the locksmith's story into a small text game in which the player is Marit. Marit Dahl has been the only locksmith in a harbour town for twenty years, and she has one rule: no proof of address, no door. On a night when a storm has cut the power, a man she has never met asks her to open a flat on Tide Street. He says it was his mother's, that she died on Tuesday, and that the landlord will clear it at eight in the morning. He has no key and no proof.

Decide for yourself what is true: what the mother's last weeks were like, whether the man is her son, and what he has come for. The player cannot ask anyone. They can only walk through the flat by torchlight and look.
essays.expectedScope: A list of four to six objects, two or three inferences and two closing sentences: 110 to 190 words. Allow about 12 minutes.
successCriteria: Lists four to six objects and says where in the flat each one is.
No object states its conclusion in words, so a note that explains everything does not count.
Names at least two things a player could infer, and each inference rests on objects in the list.
Names the kind of narrative in Jenkins's terms, and the name fits a story placed in a space for the player to find.
Names the clue that the player's next action depends on and puts it where a player who skips every cutscene still meets it.

essays.title: A branching plan and its cost
essays.prompt:
Plan the branching of the locksmith game from the doorstep to an ending. Use two decisions of three options each and at least one bottleneck. List every passage with a line on what happens in it, then count your passages, compare the count with a pure tree for the same two decisions, and give the writing cost of each at 150 words a passage.

He says it was his mother's, that she died on Tuesday, and that the landlord will clear it at eight in the morning. He has no key and no proof.

The first decision comes on the doorstep, where Marit can open the door, refuse, or ask the man for something. Choose the second decision and its options yourself.
essays.expectedScope: A list of passages and three lines of arithmetic: 110 to 190 words. Allow about 12 minutes.
successCriteria: Every passage in the plan has a line saying what happens in it.
At least one passage is reached from several options, and the plan calls it a bottleneck.
The count of passages matches the list.

At least two endings differ because of something the player chose.

essays.title: One passage for four histories
essays.prompt:
Write the passage in which Marit kneels at the lock of the flat, so that one passage serves every player. Use the two flags below, with a sentence that changes for each, and write both versions of each changing sentence inside curly braces with a vertical bar between them. Then say where each flag is set, how many states the two flags give, and which later line reads each flag.

essays.title: Barks, a quest entry and a button label
essays.prompt:
Write three kinds of text for the locksmith game: six barks, one quest log entry and one button label.

From this lesson on, the tasks turn the locksmith's story into a small text game in which the player is Marit. Marit Dahl has been the only locksmith in a harbour town for twenty years, and she has one rule: no proof of address, no door. On a night when a storm has cut the power, a man she has never met asks her to open a flat on Tide Street. He says it was his mother's, that she died on Tuesday, and that the landlord will clear it at eight in the morning. He has no key and no proof.

The barks are Marit's, spoken under her breath whenever a pick slips while the player works the lock, which can happen twenty times in one attempt. Another sound often cuts a bark off after its first two or three words.

The quest log entry is the one the player sees once the door is open. In your version of the story, decide what the player has to find or do in the flat and why it cannot wait.

The button starts the lock picking. It holds 14 characters, spaces included, and the game will be translated into French and German.
essays.expectedScope: Six barks, a quest entry of one or two sentences and a label: 50 to 100 words. Allow about 10 minutes.
successCriteria: The six barks differ from one another in wording, and none runs past about eight words.
Each bark puts the words that matter first, so that it still works when it is cut off.
The quest entry names an action, an object and a place, and gives a reason to act now.
The quest entry makes sense to a player who has skipped every cutscene.
The label is short enough to leave room in the button for a translation about a third longer.

essays.title: A vignette built on one choice
essays.prompt:
Write the opening of a vignette that ends on a choice of three options, and plan the rest. Write the shared opening in full. Then give a sentence on where each option leads, one line of reactive text that a later passage would show for one of the options, and a word budget for the whole vignette that stays within 600 words.

The budget lists the opening, each branch and any shared passage, and its total is right and within 600 words.
